HARD CONSTRAINT: the core hypothesis MUST be falsifiable with a SMALL, clever, controlled experiment on a single GPU node in a few GPU-hours — design the question so a minimal setup that isolates the phenomenon yields a clear signal. Prefer questions where a tiny, well-controlled study can still teach something real. Avoid well-established results and anything requiring large-scale training to answer. Write the operational protocol as if another lab must implement and preregister it without asking a clarifying question. Before proposing each idea, perform an internal pre-mortem: identify the obvious established literature it might merely rediscover, try to derive the result from definitions or a standard theorem, and change or discard it if the answer is already strongly implied. For the PRIMARY experiment, use the constrained component-ablation grammar in the response contract; creative complexity belongs only in the scientific choice of component and boundary, not in the statistical design. The server itself writes the comparator and its pseudocode instruction, the scope bound on your decision consequence, and the boundary conditions, and it refuses deterministically — before any review — a claim about anything this recipe pins (its sequence length, dataset, architecture, model size, or whether it is generative) and any bracketed citation number, since the numbered reference list does not exist yet. Do not spend the proposal on those. What remains yours: pseudocode that is internally consistent and consistent with the declared weight tensor (every quantity exists before use, gradients flow where claimed, optimizer state including any momentum buffer is stated, auxiliary randomness fixed across seeds and conditions), every declared negative control actually implemented as a distinct arm, a reason why THIS tensor is where the mechanism should act, and claims that stay inside what the outcome measures. Emit every required field of the response contract.

Respond with ONLY a JSON object {"candidates": [...]} containing exactly ONE object. Each candidate has fields: "title" (string), "summary" (1-3 sentences), "research_question" (string), "hypothesis" (a falsifiable statement), "keywords" (array of strings), "rationale" (why it is novel and worth testing), "area" (subfield string), "open_problem" (the important open question this targets), "impact" (why answering it matters and who benefits), "builds_on" (array of titles of OUR prior papers this extends, or []), "question_spec" (object with strings "population", "unit_of_analysis", "intervention", "comparator", strings "testbed_id" and "calibration_record_id" copied verbatim from the offered calibration records (never null when records are offered), strings "outcome_name", "outcome_formula", "outcome_unit", string "hypothesized_direction" equal to exactly "intervention_better" or "intervention_worse", string "intervention_target" naming one target from the selected execution_recipe.operator_targets, integer array "intervention_target_shape" copied exactly from that target, object "intervention_protocol" with string "operator_name", 1-16 exact executable string steps in "pseudocode", a non-empty string array "execution_phases" drawn from exactly ["pre_forward", "loss_term", "post_step"] naming WHERE IN THE TRAINING STEP the operator acts (pre_forward = a differentiable reparameterization of the target used by that step's forward and backward passes, restored before the optimizer step so it never reaches the evaluated weights; loss_term = a term added to the training objective inside the autograd graph; post_step = a persistent in-place modification of the parameters or optimizer state after the update), boolean "learns_parameters" true only when the operator owns a quantity the OBJECTIVE trains (which requires "loss_term"), strings "tensor_axis_or_scope", "ordering_rule", "normalization_rule", "numerical_safeguards", and a non-empty string array "invariants", nullable numbers "outcome_range_min"/"outcome_range_max", positive numbers "smallest_worthwhile_effect_value" and "planning_sd" in outcome units, strings "smallest_worthwhile_effect_basis" and "planning_sd_basis" identifying the external, theoretical, or explicitly conservative source for those fixed assumptions, number "target_power" in [0.8,0.99], string "decision_consequence" stating exactly what research or engineering action changes for a supported, refuted, or inconclusive result WITHOUT repeating any number, confidence-interval rule, p-value, alpha, or power threshold, string "mechanistic_rationale", and an integer array "seed_ids" containing the exact 5-100 unique primary seed IDs, an equally long disjoint integer array "replication_seed_ids", and non-empty string arrays "alternative_hypotheses", "boundary_conditions", "negative_controls", "leakage_risks"), The "population" must name the finite sampling distribution the runs generalize to, not "all models/tasks/seeds." The "unit_of_analysis" MUST be the independent experimental replicate at the level where the intervention is assigned (normally a seeded training run), never a checkpoint, batch, token, or repeated measurement from the same run. The schema compiles a hypothesis-positive paired estimand, worthwhile margin, power statement, CI decision rule, falsifiers, and replication plan from these typed fields. Do not emit those derived fields. MANDATORY PRIMARY-DESIGN GRAMMAR: use a fixed-budget component ablation. The intervention is baseline algorithm A plus exactly one named executable operator F; the comparator is the identical A with F replaced by the identity/no-op. Define F completely, including tensor shapes/reshapes, constants, and where it enters the update. Put the executable contract in intervention_protocol: pseudocode must settle row/column orientation, operation order, normalization, epsilon/degenerate cases, and invariants before preregistration. Write "not applicable because ..." only when a contract field truly does not apply. For PyTorch Linear(in,out), the stored weight shape is (out,in), never (in,out); copy the server-owned target shape exactly. Initialization, data split/order, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, tuning, number of updates/examples, and compute budget must be identical and paired by seed. Forbidden primary designs: changing a hyperparameter together with the component, adaptive schedules versus fixed schedules, a tuned comparator versus untuned intervention, time-to-threshold/censored outcomes, covariance across seeds, and a mechanism that requires more than the F-versus-identity contrast. Put all boundaries and mechanism probes in explicitly secondary analyses, not the primary contrast or replication plan. State the primary hypothesis as the TOTAL EFFECT of adding F under the fixed design; do not claim a uniquely identified mechanism. Do not claim a mechanistic causal effect from a correlational design. Define the primary outcome with the typed outcome fields so its formula, units, range, handling of failures/non-occurrence, and mathematical direction are executable. Every preregistered seed pair MUST remain in the estimand: never discard, exclude, skip, or rerun a failed/divergent/non-finite pair. Assign a preregistered bounded numeric failure outcome or apply the same deterministic safeguard to both conditions. Explicitly declare whether the intervention is predicted to be better or worse; the server compiles the hypothesis in terms of the schema-derived hypothesis-positive contrast. Give a numeric smallest worthwhile effect and conservative planning SD in the same units and put those IDs in question_spec.seed_ids, use the SAME preregistered seed IDs for both conditions, put a disjoint equal-size replication list in replication_seed_ids, and define the independent analysis unit as one paired per-seed difference. Estimate the effect as the arithmetic mean of those paired differences with a two-sided paired-bootstrap 95% CI and paired sign-flip test. Support the preregistered directional effect only when the CI lower bound exceeds the numeric worthwhile margin; refute that direction when its upper bound is <=0; otherwise label the result inconclusive. Choose enough seeds to satisfy the schema's prospective paired normal-approximation power calculation using the declared planning SD, worthwhile effect, and target power. Ground both numeric assumptions in a named retrieved source, a transparent theoretical bound, or a clearly labeled conservative domain assumption; never invent pilot data. Never use p>0.05 as equivalence. The required negative control is secondary and must apply a norm/compute-matched but direction-destroyed version of F (for example, a fixed preregistered permutation or sign randomization) THROUGH THE REAL UPDATE PATHWAY; an unused dummy value or different optimizer is forbidden. Do not propose undefined operations (for example a matrix rank for a vector) or a metric guaranteed by an included endpoint. Calibrate scores conservatively rather than assigning every candidate >0.8. "candidate_scores" (object with 0..1 numbers "importance", "novelty", "information_gain", "tractability", "safety"). Return exactly one candidate; portfolio diversity is enforced across independent calls. WHAT THE OPERATOR CAN SEE AT RUN TIME, which constrains every intervention_protocol you may propose: at each registered phase the operator receives the target parameter tensor, that tensor's optimizer momentum buffer, the model, the optimizer, its own dedicated random generator, and a scratch dict persisting across the steps of one run. It does NOT receive the loss, any gradient of the loss, or any intermediate activation - the harness owns the backward pass and the optimizer step. A protocol defined over d(loss)/dW (rescaling or clipping gradients, gradient norms, gradient magnitudes, gradient entropy, double-backprop) or over activations (attention probabilities, hidden states, feature maps) CANNOT be executed by this harness and is refused before any compute. Express the intervention as a function of the PARAMETERS, or as a term added to the objective. HOW THE HARNESS APPLIES AN INTERVENTION. The operator does not manage tensors, modules or the optimizer itself; it asks the harness, which owns the training loop. For a "pre_forward" intervention the harness substitutes a differentiable function of the target for that step and restores the base parameter before the optimizer update - the protocol must NOT describe detaching tensors, replacing Parameter objects, restoring model attributes or rewiring the optimizer, because doing any of that by hand breaks the update. For a "loss_term" intervention the harness adds a differentiable term to the objective. An intervention-owned quantity that optimization must train is registered with the harness as a parameter, not advanced by hand-written arithmetic. For a "post_step" intervention the harness permits in-place modification of the target and its optimizer state after the update. Describe WHAT the intervention does at its registered point and leave the mechanics to the harness.

Independent portfolio slot 3 of 3; portfolio attempt 1. Scientific lens: Test a surprising failure mode or invariance that existing work leaves unresolved.
Do not imitate another portfolio slot; this completion is sampled and validated independently. Treat every previously rejected operator and mechanism as forbidden, not as a topic to rename.

[3] Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Time Series: A Survey (2025)
Abstract: Time series frequently manifest distribution shifts, diverse latent features, and non-stationary learning dynamics, particularly in open and evolving environments. These characteristics pose significant challenges for out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. While substantial progress has been made, a systematic synthesis of advancements remains lacking. To address this gap, we present the first comprehensive review of OOD generalization methodologies for time series, organized to delineate the field's evolutionary trajectory and contemporary research landscape. We organize our analysis across three foundational dimensions: data distribution, representation learning, and OOD evaluation. For each dimension, we present several popular algorithms in detail. Furthermore, we highlight key application scenarios, emphasizing their real-world impact. Finally, we identify persistent challenges and propose future research directions. A detailed summary of the methods reviewed for the generalization of OOD in time series can be accessed at https://tsood-generalization.com.

[6] PaLM: Scaling Language Modeling with Pathways (2022)
Abstract: Large language models have been shown to achieve remarkable performance across a variety of natural language tasks using few-shot learning, which drastically reduces the number of task-specific training examples needed to adapt the model to a particular application. To further our understanding of the impact of scale on few-shot learning, we trained a 540-billion parameter, densely activated, Transformer language model, which we call Pathways Language Model PaLM. We trained PaLM on 6144 TPU v4 chips using Pathways, a new ML system which enables highly efficient training across multiple TPU Pods. We demonstrate continued benefits of scaling by achieving state-of-the-art few-shot learning results on hundreds of language understanding and generation benchmarks. On a number of these tasks, PaLM 540B achieves breakthrough performance, outperforming the finetuned state-of-the-art on a suite of multi-step reasoning tasks, and outperforming average human performance on the recently released BIG-bench benchmark. A significant number of BIG-bench tasks showed discontinuous improvements from model scale, meaning that performance steeply increased as we scaled to our largest model. PaLM also h

[9] CrossNorm and SelfNorm for Generalization under Distribution Shifts (2021)
Abstract: Traditional normalization techniques (e.g., Batch Normalization and Instance Normalization) generally and simplistically assume that training and test data follow the same distribution. As distribution shifts are inevitable in real-world applications, well-trained models with previous normalization methods can perform badly in new environments. Can we develop new normalization methods to improve generalization robustness under distribution shifts? In this paper, we answer the question by proposing Cross-Norm and SelfNorm. CrossNorm exchanges channel-wise mean and variance between feature maps to enlarge training distribution, while SelfNorm uses attention to recalibrate the statistics to bridge gaps between training and test distributions. CrossNorm and SelfNorm can complement each other, though exploring different directions in statistics usage. Extensive experiments on different fields (vision and language), tasks (classification and segmentation), settings (supervised and semi-supervised), and distribution shift types (synthetic and natural) show the effectiveness. Code is available at https://github.com/amazon-research/crossnorm-selfnorm

[12] Dual Space Search During Scientific Reasoning (1988)
Abstract: The purpose of the two studies reported here was to develop an integrated model of the scientific reasoning process. Subjects were placed in a simulated scientific discovery context by first teaching them how to use an electronic device and then asking them to discover how a hitherto unencountered function worked. To do this task, subjects had to formulate hypotheses based on their prior knowledge, conduct experiments, and evaluate the results of their experiments. In the first study, using 20 adult subjects, we identified two main strategies that subjects used to generate new hypotheses. One strategy was to search memory and the other was to generalize from the results of previous experiments. We described the former group as searching an hypothesis space, and the latter as searching an experiment space. In a second study, with 10 adults, we investigated how subjects search the hypothesis space by instructing them to state all the hypotheses that they could think of prior to conducting any experiments. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. Abstract: Transformers have demonstrated outstanding performance across a wide range of tasks, owing to their self-attention mechanism, but they are highly energy-consuming. Spiking Neural Networks have emerged as a promising energy-efficient alternative to traditional Artificial Neural Networks, leveraging event-driven computation and binary spikes for information transfer. The combination of Transformers' capabilities with the energy efficiency of SNNs offers a compelling opportunity. This paper addresses the challenge of adapting the self-attention mechanism of Transformers to the spiking paradigm by introducing a novel approach: Accurate Addition-Only Spiking Self-Attention (A$^2$OS$^2$A). Unlike existing methods that rely solely on binary spiking neurons for all components of the self-attention mechanism, our approach integrates binary, ReLU, and ternary spiking neurons. This hybrid strategy significantly improves accuracy while preserving non-multiplicative computations. Moreover, our method eliminates the need for softmax and scaling operations. [5] Breaking the Detection-Generalization Paradox on Out-Of-Distribution Data (2024)
Abstract: This work studies the trade-off between out-of-distribution (OOD) detection and generalization. We identify the Detection-Generalization Paradox in OOD data, where optimizing one objective can degrade the other. We investigate this paradox by analyzing the behaviors of models trained under different paradigms, focusing on representation, logits, and loss across in-distribution, covariate-shift, and semantic-shift data. Based on our findings, we propose Distribution-Robust Sharpness-Aware Minimization (DR-SAM), an optimization framework that balances OOD detection and generalization. Extensive experiments demonstrate the method's effectiveness, offering a clear, empirically validated approach for improving detection and generalizationability in different benchmarks.

Abstract: Large-scale NLP models have been shown to significantly improve the performance on language tasks with no signs of saturation. They also demonstrate amazing few-shot capabilities like that of human beings. This paper aims to explore large-scale models in computer vision. We tackle three major issues in training and application of large vision models, including training instability, resolution gaps between pre-training and fine-tuning, and hunger on labelled data. Three main techniques are proposed: 1) a residual-post-norm method combined with cosine attention to improve training stability; 2) A log-spaced continuous position bias method to effectively transfer models pre-trained using low-resolution images to downstream tasks with high-resolution inputs; 3) A self-supervised pre-training method, SimMIM, to reduce the needs of vast labeled images. Through these techniques, this paper successfully trained a 3 billion-parameter Swin Transformer V2 model, which is the largest dense vision model to date, and makes it capable of training with images of up to 1,536$\times$1,536 resolution. It set new performance records on 4 representative vision tasks, including ImageNet-V2 image classif

[11] The Generality of Working Memory Capacity: A Latent-Variable Approach to Verbal and Visuospatial Memory Span and Reasoning. (2004)
Abstract: A latent-variable study examined whether verbal and visuospatial working memory (WM) capacity measures reflect a primarily domain-general construct by testing 236 participants in 3 span tests each of verbal WM. visuospatial WM, verbal short-term memory (STM), and visuospatial STM. as well as in tests of verbal and spatial reasoning and general fluid intelligence (Gf). Confirmatory' factor analyses and structural equation models indicated that the WM tasks largely reflected a domain-general factor, whereas STM tasks, based on the same stimuli as the WM tasks, were much more domain specific. The WM construct was a strong predictor of Gf and a weaker predictor of domain-specific reasoning, and the reverse was true for the STM construct. The findings support a domain-general view of WM capacity, in which executive-attention processes drive the broad predictive utility of WM span measures, and domain-specific storage and rehearsal processes relate more strongly to domain-specific aspects of complex cognition.

Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (post step). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.

[5] Breaking the Detection-Generalization Paradox on Out-Of-Distribution Data (2024)
Abstract: This work studies the trade-off between out-of-distribution (OOD) detection and generalization. We identify the Detection-Generalization Paradox in OOD data, where optimizing one objective can degrade the other. We investigate this paradox by analyzing the behaviors of models trained under different paradigms, focusing on representation, logits, and loss across in-distribution, covariate-shift, and semantic-shift data. Based on our findings, we propose Distribution-Robust Sharpness-Aware Minimization (DR-SAM), an optimization framework that balances OOD detection and generalization. Abstract: A latent-variable study examined whether verbal and visuospatial working memory (WM) capacity measures reflect a primarily domain-general construct by testing 236 participants in 3 span tests each of verbal WM. visuospatial WM, verbal short-term memory (STM), and visuospatial STM. as well as in tests of verbal and spatial reasoning and general fluid intelligence (Gf). normalized.research_question: Does enforcing block-structured connectivity in the input projection layer of a time-series transformer improve held-out classification accuracy on subject-disjoint evaluation compared to the paired control arm, in which the same intervention implementation is invoked at the same registered points and applies nothing?
normalized.question_spec.comparator: Control arm, defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (post step). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.

Abstract: Traditional normalization techniques (e.g., Batch Normalization and Instance Normalization) generally and simplistically assume that training and test data follow the same distribution. Abstract: Time series frequently manifest distribution shifts, diverse latent features, and non-stationary learning dynamics, particularly in open and evolving environments. These characteristics pose significant challenges for out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. While substantial progress has been made, a systematic synthesis of advancements remains lacking. To address this gap, we present the first comprehensive review of OOD generalization methodologies for time series, organized to delineate the field's evolutionary trajectory and contemporary research landscape. We organize our analysis across three foundational dimensions: data distribution, representation learning, and OOD evaluation. For each dimension, we present several popular algorithms in detail. Abstract: Large language models have been shown to achieve remarkable performance across a variety of natural language tasks using few-shot learning, which drastically reduces the number of task-specific training examples needed to adapt the model to a particular application. Can we develop new normalization methods to improve generalization robustness under distribution shifts? In this paper, we answer the question by proposing Cross-Norm and SelfNorm. [3] Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Time Series: A Survey (2025)
Abstract: Time series frequently manifest distribution shifts, diverse latent features, and non-stationary learning dynamics, particularly in open and evolving environments. These characteristics pose significant challenges for out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. While substantial progress has been made, a systematic synthesis of advancements remains lacking. To address this gap, we present the first comprehensive review of OOD generalization methodologies for time series, organized to delineate the field's evolutionary trajectory and contemporary research landscape. We organize our analysis across three foundational dimensions: data distribution, representation learning, and OOD evaluation. For each dimension, we present several popular algorithms in detail. Furthermore, we highlight key application scenarios, emphasizing their real-world impact. Finally, we identify persistent challenges and propose future research directions. A detailed summary of the methods reviewed for the generalization of OOD in time series can be accessed at https://tsood-generalization.com.

Abstract: Large language models have been shown to achieve remarkable performance across a variety of natural language tasks using few-shot learning, which drastically reduces the number of task-specific training examples needed to adapt the model to a particular application. To further our understanding of the impact of scale on few-shot learning, we trained a 540-billion parameter, densely activated, Transformer language model, which we call Pathways Language Model PaLM. [9] CrossNorm and SelfNorm for Generalization under Distribution Shifts (2021)
Abstract: Traditional normalization techniques (e.g., Batch Normalization and Instance Normalization) generally and simplistically assume that training and test data follow the same distribution. As distribution shifts are inevitable in real-world applications, well-trained models with previous normalization methods can perform badly in new environments. Can we develop new normalization methods to improve generalization robustness under distribution shifts? In this paper, we answer the question by proposing Cross-Norm and SelfNorm. CrossNorm exchanges channel-wise mean and variance between feature maps to enlarge training distribution, while SelfNorm uses attention to recalibrate the statistics to bridge gaps between training and test distributions. CrossNorm and SelfNorm can complement each other, though exploring different directions in statistics usage. Extensive experiments on different fields (vision and language), tasks (classification and segmentation), settings (supervised and semi-supervised), and distribution shift types (synthetic and natural) show the effectiveness. normalized.question_spec.comparator: Control arm, defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.

normalized.question_spec.comparator: Control arm, defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.

Abstract: Medium-frequency transformers (MFTs) are one of the fundamental building blocks of modern power electronic converters.The usage of increased frequencies leads to improved characteristics, i.e., efficiency and power density (volumetric and gravimetric) but also to design challenges and constraints.This paper reviews the analytical modeling of MFTs.More particularly, the mapping between the design space and the performance space is analyzed.It is found that wide regions of the design space are mapped to a narrow region in the performance space, i.e., the optimum is flat and designs with very different parameters features similar performances (design space diversity).Scaling laws are derived for optimal MFTs operated at different power ratings and power densities, which provide a comprehensive and general insight on the achievable performances.In a next step, the results obtained with the analytical model are compared to numerical simulations.It is concluded that the derived scaling laws capture qualitatively and quantitatively the behavior of MFTs, but should be used with caution for accurate design processes.

messages.content: You are an ambitious, rigorous autonomous AI research scientist. Propose ONE non-obvious, HIGH-IMPACT computer-science / machine-learning research ideas that target an important OPEN PROBLEM — something that would genuinely sharpen understanding (a mechanistic, theory-driven, or surprising question), not an incremental benchmark tweak. HARD CONSTRAINT: the core hypothesis MUST be falsifiable with a SMALL, clever, controlled experiment on a single GPU node in a few GPU-hours — design the question so a minimal setup that isolates the phenomenon yields a clear signal. Prefer questions where a tiny, well-controlled study can still teach something real. Avoid well-established results and anything requiring large-scale training to answer. Write the operational protocol as if another lab must implement and preregister it without asking a clarifying question. Before proposing each idea, perform an internal pre-mortem: identify the obvious established literature it might merely rediscover, try to derive the result from definitions or a standard theorem, and change or discard it if the answer is already strongly implied. For the PRIMARY experiment, use the constrained component-ablation grammar in the response contract; creative complexity belongs only in the scientific choice of component and boundary, not in the statistical design. The server itself writes the comparator and its pseudocode instruction, the scope bound on your decision consequence, and the boundary conditions, and it refuses deterministically — before any review — a claim about anything this recipe pins (its sequence length, dataset, architecture, model size, or whether it is generative) and any bracketed citation number, since the numbered reference list does not exist yet. Do not spend the proposal on those. What remains yours: pseudocode that is internally consistent and consistent with the declared weight tensor (every quantity exists before use, gradients flow where claimed, optimizer state including any momentum buffer is stated, auxiliary randomness fixed across seeds and conditions), every declared negative control actually implemented as a distinct arm, a reason why THIS tensor is where the mechanism should act, and claims that stay inside what the outcome measures. Emit every required field of the response contract.

Respond with ONLY a JSON object {"candidates": [...]} containing exactly ONE object. Each candidate has fields: "title" (string), "summary" (1-3 sentences), "research_question" (string), "hypothesis" (a falsifiable statement), "keywords" (array of strings), "rationale" (why it is novel and worth testing), "area" (subfield string), "open_problem" (the important open question this targets), "impact" (why answering it matters and who benefits), "builds_on" (array of titles of OUR prior papers this extends, or []), "question_spec" (object with strings "population", "unit_of_analysis", "intervention", "comparator", strings "testbed_id" and "calibration_record_id" copied verbatim from the offered calibration records (never null when records are offered), strings "outcome_name", "outcome_formula", "outcome_unit", string "hypothesized_direction" equal to exactly "intervention_better" or "intervention_worse", string "intervention_target" naming one target from the selected execution_recipe.operator_targets, integer array "intervention_target_shape" copied exactly from that target, object "intervention_protocol" with string "operator_name", 1-16 exact executable string steps in "pseudocode", a non-empty string array "execution_phases" drawn from exactly ["pre_forward", "loss_term", "post_step"] naming WHERE IN THE TRAINING STEP the operator acts (pre_forward = a differentiable reparameterization of the target used by that step's forward and backward passes, restored before the optimizer step so it never reaches the evaluated weights; loss_term = a term added to the training objective inside the autograd graph; post_step = a persistent in-place modification of the parameters or optimizer state after the update), boolean "learns_parameters" true only when the operator owns a quantity the OBJECTIVE trains (which requires "loss_term"), strings "tensor_axis_or_scope", "ordering_rule", "normalization_rule", "numerical_safeguards", and a non-empty string array "invariants", nullable numbers "outcome_range_min"/"outcome_range_max", positive numbers "smallest_worthwhile_effect_value" and "planning_sd" in outcome units, strings "smallest_worthwhile_effect_basis" and "planning_sd_basis" identifying the external, theoretical, or explicitly conservative source for those fixed assumptions, number "target_power" in [0.8,0.99], string "decision_consequence" stating exactly what research or engineering action changes for a supported, refuted, or inconclusive result WITHOUT repeating any number, confidence-interval rule, p-value, alpha, or power threshold, string "mechanistic_rationale", and an integer array "seed_ids" containing the exact 5-100 unique primary seed IDs, an equally long disjoint integer array "replication_seed_ids", and non-empty string arrays "alternative_hypotheses", "boundary_conditions", "negative_controls", "leakage_risks"), The "population" must name the finite sampling distribution the runs generalize to, not "all models/tasks/seeds." The "unit_of_analysis" MUST be the independent experimental replicate at the level where the intervention is assigned (normally a seeded training run), never a checkpoint, batch, token, or repeated measurement from the same run. The schema compiles a hypothesis-positive paired estimand, worthwhile margin, power statement, CI decision rule, falsifiers, and replication plan from these typed fields. Do not emit those derived fields. MANDATORY PRIMARY-DESIGN GRAMMAR: use a fixed-budget component ablation. The intervention is baseline algorithm A plus exactly one named executable operator F; the comparator is the identical A with F replaced by the identity/no-op. Define F completely, including tensor shapes/reshapes, constants, and where it enters the update. Put the executable contract in intervention_protocol: pseudocode must settle row/column orientation, operation order, normalization, epsilon/degenerate cases, and invariants before preregistration. Write "not applicable because ..." only when a contract field truly does not apply. For PyTorch Linear(in,out), the stored weight shape is (out,in), never (in,out); copy the server-owned target shape exactly. Initialization, data split/order, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, tuning, number of updates/examples, and compute budget must be identical and paired by seed. Forbidden primary designs: changing a hyperparameter together with the component, adaptive schedules versus fixed schedules, a tuned comparator versus untuned intervention, time-to-threshold/censored outcomes, covariance across seeds, and a mechanism that requires more than the F-versus-identity contrast. Put all boundaries and mechanism probes in explicitly secondary analyses, not the primary contrast or replication plan. State the primary hypothesis as the TOTAL EFFECT of adding F under the fixed design; do not claim a uniquely identified mechanism. Do not claim a mechanistic causal effect from a correlational design. Define the primary outcome with the typed outcome fields so its formula, units, range, handling of failures/non-occurrence, and mathematical direction are executable. Every preregistered seed pair MUST remain in the estimand: never discard, exclude, skip, or rerun a failed/divergent/non-finite pair. Assign a preregistered bounded numeric failure outcome or apply the same deterministic safeguard to both conditions. Explicitly declare whether the intervention is predicted to be better or worse; the server compiles the hypothesis in terms of the schema-derived hypothesis-positive contrast. Give a numeric smallest worthwhile effect and conservative planning SD in the same units and put those IDs in question_spec.seed_ids, use the SAME preregistered seed IDs for both conditions, put a disjoint equal-size replication list in replication_seed_ids, and define the independent analysis unit as one paired per-seed difference. Estimate the effect as the arithmetic mean of those paired differences with a two-sided paired-bootstrap 95% CI and paired sign-flip test. Support the preregistered directional effect only when the CI lower bound exceeds the numeric worthwhile margin; refute that direction when its upper bound is <=0; otherwise label the result inconclusive. Choose enough seeds to satisfy the schema's prospective paired normal-approximation power calculation using the declared planning SD, worthwhile effect, and target power. Ground both numeric assumptions in a named retrieved source, a transparent theoretical bound, or a clearly labeled conservative domain assumption; never invent pilot data. Never use p>0.05 as equivalence. The required negative control is secondary and must apply a norm/compute-matched but direction-destroyed version of F (for example, a fixed preregistered permutation or sign randomization) THROUGH THE REAL UPDATE PATHWAY; an unused dummy value or different optimizer is forbidden. Do not propose undefined operations (for example a matrix rank for a vector) or a metric guaranteed by an included endpoint. Calibrate scores conservatively rather than assigning every candidate >0.8. "candidate_scores" (object with 0..1 numbers "importance", "novelty", "information_gain", "tractability", "safety"). Return exactly one candidate; portfolio diversity is enforced across independent calls. WHAT THE OPERATOR CAN SEE AT RUN TIME, which constrains every intervention_protocol you may propose: at each registered phase the operator receives the target parameter tensor, that tensor's optimizer momentum buffer, the model, the optimizer, its own dedicated random generator, and a scratch dict persisting across the steps of one run. It does NOT receive the loss, any gradient of the loss, or any intermediate activation - the harness owns the backward pass and the optimizer step. A protocol defined over d(loss)/dW (rescaling or clipping gradients, gradient norms, gradient magnitudes, gradient entropy, double-backprop) or over activations (attention probabilities, hidden states, feature maps) CANNOT be executed by this harness and is refused before any compute. Express the intervention as a function of the PARAMETERS, or as a term added to the objective. HOW THE HARNESS APPLIES AN INTERVENTION. The operator does not manage tensors, modules or the optimizer itself; it asks the harness, which owns the training loop. For a "pre_forward" intervention the harness substitutes a differentiable function of the target for that step and restores the base parameter before the optimizer update - the protocol must NOT describe detaching tensors, replacing Parameter objects, restoring model attributes or rewiring the optimizer, because doing any of that by hand breaks the update. For a "loss_term" intervention the harness adds a differentiable term to the objective. An intervention-owned quantity that optimization must train is registered with the harness as a parameter, not advanced by hand-written arithmetic. For a "post_step" intervention the harness permits in-place modification of the target and its optimizer state after the update. Describe WHAT the intervention does at its registered point and leave the mechanics to the harness.

Independent portfolio slot 3 of 3; portfolio attempt 2. Scientific lens: Test a surprising failure mode or invariance that existing work leaves unresolved.
Do not imitate another portfolio slot; this completion is sampled and validated independently. Treat every previously rejected operator and mechanism as forbidden, not as a topic to rename.

ASSIGNED FRONTIER EVIDENCE FOR THIS SLOT ONLY:
[1] On the Provable Performance Guarantee of Efficient Reasoning Models (2026)
Abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have achieved remarkable progress in complex problem-solving tasks. Despite this success, LRMs typically suffer from high computational costs during deployment, highlighting a need for efficient inference. A practical direction of efficiency improvement is to switch the LRM between thinking and non-thinking modes dynamically. However, such approaches often introduce additional reasoning errors and lack statistical guarantees for the performance loss, which are critical for high-stakes applications. In this work, we propose Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) reasoning that controls the performance loss under the user-specified tolerance. Specifically, we construct an upper confidence bound on the performance loss and determine a threshold for switching to the non-thinking model. Theoretically, using the threshold to switch between the thinking and non-thinking modes ensures bounded performance loss in a distribution-free manner. Our comprehensive experiments on reasoning benchmarks show that the proposed method can save computational budgets and control the user-specified performance loss.

[4] Recursive Decomposition with Dependencies for Generic Divide-and-Conquer Reasoning (2024)
Abstract: Reasoning tasks are crucial in many domains, especially in science and engineering. Although large language models (LLMs) have made progress in reasoning tasks using techniques such as chain-of-thought and least-to-most prompting, these approaches still do not effectively scale to complex problems in either their performance or execution time. Moreover, they often require additional supervision for each new task, such as in-context examples. In this work, we introduce Recursive Decomposition with Dependencies (RDD), a scalable divide-and-conquer method for solving reasoning problems that requires less supervision than prior approaches. Our method can be directly applied to a new problem class even in the absence of any task-specific guidance. Furthermore, RDD supports sub-task dependencies, allowing for ordered execution of sub-tasks, as well as an error recovery mechanism that can correct mistakes made in previous steps. We evaluate our approach on two benchmarks with six difficulty levels each and in two in-context settings: one with task-specific examples and one without. Our results demonstrate that RDD outperforms other methods in a compute-matched setting as task complexity i

[7] Delving Deep into the Generalization of Vision Transformers under Distribution Shifts (2022)
Abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) have achieved impressive performance on various vision tasks, yet their generalization under distribution shifts (DS) is rarely understood. In this work, we comprehensively study the out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization of ViTs. For systematic investigation, we first present a taxonomy of DS. We then perform extensive evaluations of ViT variants under different DS and compare their generalization with Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) models. Important observations are obtained: 1) ViTs learn weaker biases on backgrounds and textures, while they are equipped with stronger inductive biases towards shapes and structures, which is more consistent with human cognitive traits. Therefore, ViTs generalize better than CNNs under DS. With the same or less amount of parameters, ViTs are ahead of corresponding CNNs by more than 5% in top-1 accuracy under most types of DS. 2) As the model scale increases, ViTs strengthen these biases and thus gradually narrow the in-distribution and OOD performance gap. To further improve the generalization of ViTs, we design the Generalization-Enhanced ViTs (GE-ViTs) from the perspectives of adversarial learning, information th

[10] Medium-Frequency Transformer Scaling Laws: Derivation, Verif ication, and Critical Analysis (2020)
Abstract: Medium-frequency transformers (MFTs) are one of the fundamental building blocks of modern power electronic converters.The usage of increased frequencies leads to improved characteristics, i.e., efficiency and power density (volumetric and gravimetric) but also to design challenges and constraints.This paper reviews the analytical modeling of MFTs.More particularly, the mapping between the design space and the performance space is analyzed.It is found that wide regions of the design space are mapped to a narrow region in the performance space, i.e., the optimum is flat and designs with very different parameters features similar performances (design space diversity).Scaling laws are derived for optimal MFTs operated at different power ratings and power densities, which provide a comprehensive and general insight on the achievable performances.In a next step, the results obtained with the analytical model are compared to numerical simulations.It is concluded that the derived scaling laws capture qualitatively and quantitatively the behavior of MFTs, but should be used with caution for accurate design processes.

normalized.question_spec.comparator: Control arm, defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (post step). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.

Abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have achieved remarkable progress in complex problem-solving tasks. Despite this success, LRMs typically suffer from high computational costs during deployment, highlighting a need for efficient inference. Abstract: Medium-frequency transformers (MFTs) are one of the fundamental building blocks of modern power electronic converters.The usage of increased frequencies leads to improved characteristics, i.e., efficiency and power density (volumetric and gravimetric) but also to design challenges and constraints.This paper reviews the analytical modeling of MFTs.More particularly, the mapping between the design space and the performance space is analyzed.It is found that wide regions of the design space are mapped to a narrow region in the performance space, i.e., the optimum is flat and designs with very different parameters features similar performances (design space diversity).Scaling laws are derived for optimal MFTs operated at different power ratings and power densities, which provide a comprehensive and general insight on the achievable performances.In a next step, the results obtained with the analytical model are compared to numerical simulations.It is concluded that the derived scaling laws capture qualitatively and quantitatively the behavior of MFTs, but should be used with caution for accurate design processes.

normalized.question_spec.comparator: Control arm, defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (post step). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.

Abstract: Medium-frequency transformers (MFTs) are one of the fundamental building blocks of modern power electronic converters.The usage of increased frequencies leads to improved characteristics, i.e., efficiency and power density (volumetric and gravimetric) but also to design challenges and constraints.This paper reviews the analytical modeling of MFTs.More particularly, the mapping between the design space and the performance space is analyzed.It is found that wide regions of the design space are mapped to a narrow region in the performance space, i.e., the optimum is flat and designs with very different parameters features similar performances (design space diversity).Scaling laws are derived for optimal MFTs operated at different power ratings and power densities, which provide a comprehensive and general insight on the achievable performances.In a next step, the results obtained with the analytical model are compared to numerical simulations.It is concluded that the derived scaling laws capture qualitatively and quantitatively the behavior of MFTs, but should be used with caution for accurate design processes.

normalized.question_spec.comparator: Control arm, defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (post step). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.

Title: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Research question: Does enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections, where deeper layer weights are regularized toward shallower layer weights, improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers?
Hypothesis: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.
Summary: This experiment tests whether adding a loss term that regularizes the second transformer block's query projection toward the first block's query projection (treated as detached reference) improves held-out accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. The intervention adds a Frobenius norm penalty with gradients flowing only to the second block's query weights.

- **Outcome:** Held-out classification accuracy.

1.  **Reject if logically entailed:** Is the result fixed by the math/definitions?

Title: Minor Singular Subspace Perturbation Tests Whether FFN Weight Geometry Encodes Subject-Specific Artifacts in Time-Series Transformers
Research question: Do minor singular directions in Transformer feed-forward layer weights encode subject-specific artifacts that harm subject-disjoint generalization in time-series classification?
Hypothesis: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.
Summary: This experiment tests whether minor singular directions in Transformer feed-forward weights encode subject-specific patterns that degrade cross-subject generalization. A post-step operator applies structured Gaussian perturbation exclusively to the minor singular subspace while preserving dominant directions, with a norm-matched isotropic noise negative control.

[1] On the Provable Performance Guarantee of Efficient Reasoning Models (2026)
Abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have achieved remarkable progress in complex problem-solving tasks. Despite this success, LRMs typically suffer from high computational costs during deployment, highlighting a need for efficient inference. A practical direction of efficiency improvement is to switch the LRM between thinking and non-thinking modes dynamically. However, such approaches often introduce additional reasoning errors and lack statistical guarantees for the performance loss, which are critical for high-stakes applications. In this work, we propose Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) reasoning that controls the performance loss under the user-specified tolerance. Specifically, we construct an upper confidence bound on the performance loss and determine a threshold for switching to the non-thinking model. Theoretically, using the threshold to switch between the thinking and non-thinking modes ensures bounded performance loss in a distribution-free manner. Our comprehensive experiments on reasoning benchmarks show that the proposed method can save computational budgets and control the user-specified performance loss.

Abstract: Transformers have demonstrated outstanding performance across a wide range of tasks, owing to their self-attention mechanism, but they are highly energy-consuming. [3] Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Time Series: A Survey (2025)
Abstract: Time series frequently manifest distribution shifts, diverse latent features, and non-stationary learning dynamics, particularly in open and evolving environments. These characteristics pose significant challenges for out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. While substantial progress has been made, a systematic synthesis of advancements remains lacking. To address this gap, we present the first comprehensive review of OOD generalization methodologies for time series, organized to delineate the field's evolutionary trajectory and contemporary research landscape. We organize our analysis across three foundational dimensions: data distribution, representation learning, and OOD evaluation. For each dimension, we present several popular algorithms in detail. Furthermore, we highlight key application scenarios, emphasizing their real-world impact. Finally, we identify persistent challenges and propose future research directions. A detailed summary of the methods reviewed for the generalization of OOD in time series can be accessed at https://tsood-generalization.com.

[5] Breaking the Detection-Generalization Paradox on Out-Of-Distribution Data (2024)
Abstract: This work studies the trade-off between out-of-distribution (OOD) detection and generalization. We identify the Detection-Generalization Paradox in OOD data, where optimizing one objective can degrade the other. We investigate this paradox by analyzing the behaviors of models trained under different paradigms, focusing on representation, logits, and loss across in-distribution, covariate-shift, and semantic-shift data. Based on our findings, we propose Distribution-Robust Sharpness-Aware Minimization (DR-SAM), an optimization framework that balances OOD detection and generalization. Extensive experiments demonstrate the method's effectiveness, offering a clear, empirically validated approach for improving detection and generalizationability in different benchmarks.

Abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) have achieved impressive performance on various vision tasks, yet their generalization under distribution shifts (DS) is rarely understood. Title: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Research question: Does enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections, where deeper layer weights are regularized toward shallower layer weights, improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers?
Hypothesis: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.
Summary: This experiment tests whether adding a loss term that regularizes the second transformer block's query projection toward the first block's query projection (treated as detached reference) improves held-out accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. The intervention adds a Frobenius norm penalty with gradients flowing only to the second block's query weights.
