[26] Transformers in Remote Sensing: A Survey
Abstract: Deep learning-based algorithms have seen a massive popularity in different areas of remote sensing image analysis over the past decade. Recently, transformer-based architectures, originally introduced in natural language processing, have pervaded computer vision field where the self-attention mechanism has been utilized as a replacement to the popular convolution operator for capturing long-range dependencies. Inspired by recent advances in computer vision, the remote sensing community has also witnessed an increased exploration of vision transformers for a diverse set of tasks. Although a number of surveys have focused on transformers in computer vision in general, to the best of our knowledge we are the first to present a systematic review of recent advances based on transformers in remote sensing. Our survey covers more than 60 recent transformer-based methods for different remote sensing problems in sub-areas of remote sensing: very high-resolution (VHR), hyperspectral (HSI) and synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery. We conclude the survey by discussing different challenges and open issues of transformers in remote sensing.

[27] Transformer Architecture and Attention Mechanisms in Genome Data Analysis: A Comprehensive Review
Abstract: The emergence and rapid development of deep learning, specifically transformer-based architectures and attention mechanisms, have had transformative implications across several domains, including bioinformatics and genome data analysis. The analogous nature of genome sequences to language texts has enabled the application of techniques that have exhibited success in fields ranging from natural language processing to genomic data. This review provides a comprehensive analysis of the most recent advancements in the application of transformer architectures and attention mechanisms to genome and transcriptome data. The focus of this review is on the critical evaluation of these techniques, discussing their advantages and limitations in the context of genome data analysis. With the swift pace of development in deep learning methodologies, it becomes vital to continually assess and reflect on the current standing and future direction of the research. Therefore, this review aims to serve as a timely resource for both seasoned researchers and newcomers, offering a panoramic view of the recent advancements and elucidating the state-of-the-art applications in the field. Furthermore, this review paper serves to highlight potential areas of future investigation by critically evaluating studies from 2019 to 2023, thereby acting as a stepping-stone for further research endeavors.

Motivated by this insight, we introduce a novel approach called Series2Vec for self-supervised representation learning. Unlike the state-of-the-art methods in time series which rely on hand-crafted data augmentation, Series2Vec is trained by predicting the similarity between two series in both temporal and spectral domains through a self-supervised task. By leveraging the similarity prediction task, which has inherent meaning for a wide range of time series analysis tasks, Series2Vec eliminates the need for hand-crafted data augmentation. To further enforce the network to learn similar representations for similar time series, we propose a novel approach that applies order-invariant attention to each representation within the batch during training. Our evaluation of Series2Vec on nine large real-world datasets, along with the UCR/UEA archive, shows enhanced performance compared to current state-of-the-art self-supervised techniques for time series. Additionally, our extensive experiments show that Series2Vec performs comparably with fully supervised training and offers high efficiency in datasets with limited-labeled data. Finally, we show that the fusion of Series2Vec with other representation learning models leads to enhanced performance for time series classification. Code and mo […abstract truncated here]

[29] Attention mechanisms in computer vision: A survey
Abstract: Humans can naturally and effectively find salient regions in complex scenes. Motivated by this observation, attention mechanisms were introduced into computer vision with the aim of imitating this aspect of the human visual system. Such an attention mechanism can be regarded as a dynamic weight adjustment process based on features of the input image. Attention mechanisms have achieved great success in many visual tasks, including image classification, object detection, semantic segmentation, video understanding, image generation, 3D vision, multimodal tasks, and self-supervised learning. In this survey, we provide a comprehensive review of various attention mechanisms in computer vision and categorize them according to approach, such as channel attention, spatial attention, temporal attention, and branch attention; a related repository https://github.com/MenghaoGuo/Awesome-Vision-Attentions is dedicated to collecting related work. We also suggest future directions for attention mechanism research.

[30] Anomaly Transformer: Time Series Anomaly Detection with Association Discrepancy
Abstract: Anomaly detection in time series data is a critical task in various domains, including finance, healthcare, cybersecurity and industry. Traditional methods, such as time series decomposition, clustering, and density estimation, have provided robust solutions for identifying anomalies that exhibit distinct patterns or significant deviations from normal data distributions. Recent advancements in machine learning and deep learning have further enhanced these capabilities. This paper introduces a novel method for anomaly detection that combines the strengths of autoencoders and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with an reconstruction error feedback mechanism based on Mean Squared Error. We compare our method against classical techniques and recent approaches like OmniAnomaly, which leverages stochastic recurrent neural networks, and the Anomaly Transformer, which introduces association discrepancy to capture long-range dependencies and DCDetector using contrastive representation learning with multi-scale dual attention. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves superior overall performance in terms of precision, recall, and F1 score. The source code is available at http://github.com/mribrahim/AE-FAR

[31] Neural Speech Synthesis with Transformer Network
Abstract: Although end-to-end neural text-to-speech (TTS) methods (such as Tacotron2) are proposed and achieve state-of-theart performance, they still suffer from two problems: 1) low efficiency during training and inference; 2) hard to model long dependency using current recurrent neural networks (RNNs). Inspired by the success of Transformer network in neural machine translation (NMT), in this paper, we introduce and adapt the multi-head attention mechanism to replace the RNN structures and also the original attention mechanism in Tacotron2. With the help of multi-head self-attention, the hidden states in the encoder and decoder are constructed in parallel, which improves training efficiency. Meanwhile, any two inputs at different times are connected directly by a self-attention mechanism, which solves the long range dependency problem effectively. Using phoneme sequences as input, our Transformer TTS network generates mel spectrograms, followed by a WaveNet vocoder to output the final audio results. Experiments are conducted to test the efficiency and performance of our new network. For the efficiency, our Transformer TTS network can speed up the training about 4.25 times faster compared with Tacotron2. For the performance, rigorous human tests show that our proposed model achieves state-of-the-art performance (outperforms Tacotron2 with a gap of 0.048) and is very close to human quality (4.39 vs 4.44 in MOS).

[32] Cross-Attention Transformer for Coherent Detection in Radar Under Low-SNR Conditions
Abstract: Detecting weak echoes from low-RCS targets in pulsed radar systems presents significant challenges, as conventional coherent accumulation methods require extended dwell times that reduce data rates and suffer from target-motion-induced migration. We propose RD-Transformer, an end-to-end attention-based architecture that reformulates coherent integration as a learned feature fusion problem. The framework integrates multi-pulse transpose preprocessing, dual-path self-attention encoders for transmitted and received signals, and a cross-attention decoder to extract transmit-receive interaction features. A tunable sigmoid-based gating mechanism enables flexible false alarm control during inference. Experiments on synthetic pulsed-radar data demonstrate that, under identical false alarm constraints (Pfa = 1 × 10−2 to 1 × 10−5) and using only 10 coherent pulses, RD-Transformer reduces the required SNR by 14–20 dB compared to optimal energy detection across Swerling I-IV target fluctuation models, validating the effectiveness of learned coherent accumulation for weak target detection.

[33] Multivariate Time Series Anomaly Detection with Fourier Time Series Transformer
Abstract: Anomaly detection in time series data plays a key role in automatic industrial operations. Due to the intricate temporal dependencies within time series data and the difficulty in obtaining labeled data, recent anomaly detection methods have primarily focused on the temporal domain features of time series data, neglecting the frequency domain features. However, spectral analysis can better utilize periodic information within time series data such as seasonal patterns, which helps capturing multi-scale and multiple frequency features. In this paper, we present a Fourier Time Series Transformer model (FTST for short), which combines the features of both time and frequency domains for time series anomaly detection. Specifically, the attention mechanism is utilized for modeling the temporal domain, while the Fourier Transform is employed to transform time series data into frequency domain data. The frequency domain features are then modeled using a Temporal Convolutional Network. By making full use of the temporal and frequency domains of time series data, FTST can significantly enhance the performance of time series anomaly detection. Experimental results on popular benchmark datasets demonstrate the anomaly detection performance of the proposed method.

[34] Attention as a Hypernetwork
Abstract: Transformers can under some circumstances generalize to novel problem instances whose constituent parts might have been encountered during training, but whose compositions have not. What mechanisms underlie this ability for compositional generalization? By reformulating multi-head attention as a hypernetwork, we reveal that a composable, low-dimensional latent code specifies key-query specific operations. We find empirically that this latent code is predictive of the subtasks the network performs on unseen task compositions, revealing that latent codes acquired during training are reused to solve unseen problem instances. To further examine the hypothesis that the intrinsic hypernetwork of multi-head attention supports compositional generalization, we ablate whether making the hypernetwork-generated linear value network nonlinear strengthens compositionality. We find that this modification improves compositional generalization on abstract reasoning tasks. In particular, we introduce a symbolic version of the Raven's Progressive Matrices human intelligence test, which gives us precise control over the problem compositions encountered during training and evaluation. We demonstrate on this task how scaling model size and data enables compositional generalization in transformers and gives rise to a functionally structured latent space.

[35] Transformers in medical image analysis
Abstract: Transformers have dominated the field of natural language processing and have recently made an impact in the area of computer vision. In the field of medical image analysis, transformers have also been successfully used in to full-stack clinical applications, including image synthesis/reconstruction, registration, segmentation, detection, and diagnosis. This paper aimed to promote awareness of the applications of transformers in medical image analysis. Specifically, we first provided an overview of the core concepts of the attention mechanism built into transformers and other basic components. Second, we reviewed various transformer architectures tailored for medical image applications and discuss their limitations. Within this review, we investigated key challenges including the use of transformers in different learning paradigms, improving model efficiency, and coupling with other techniques. We hope this review would provide a comprehensive picture of transformers to readers with an interest in medical image analysis.

[36] Contrastive Time-Series Anomaly Detection
Abstract: In addition to its success in representation learning, contrastive learning is effective in image anomaly detection. Additionally, although time-series data share a temporal context, the existing contrastive loss contrasts temporally related samples, in which deteriorated anomaly detection performance is observed on time-series data. Herein, we propose contrastive multivariate time-series anomaly detection (CTAD), a multivariate time-series anomaly detection framework that addresses these challenges by incorporating a one-class learning scheme into the contrastive loss based on meticulously designed time-series data augmentations. Specifically, we propose seven types of general time-series data augmentations to be applied variable- and point-wise, and provide guidance on data augmentation methods for contrastive time-series anomaly detection. The superiority of the one-class contrastive loss and the appropriate selection of time-series data augmentation allow CTAD to achieve outstanding performance in multiple datasets, even using a simple long short-term memory network. Furthermore, CTAD is robust to noise as it trains a noise-invariant network. This enables up to 47× faster and 20× more memory-efficient anomaly detection performance compared with existing methods while affording robustness, which are essential considera […abstract truncated here]

[37] Retrieval Augmented Time Series Forecasting
Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a central component of modern LLM systems, particularly in scenarios where up-to-date information is crucial for accurately responding to user queries or when queries exceed the scope of the training data. The advent of time-series foundation models (TSFM), such as Chronos or Moirai, and the need for effective zero-shot forecasting performance across various time-series domains motivates the question: Do the benefits of RAG similarly carry over to time series forecasting? In this paper, we advocate that the dynamic and event-driven nature of time-series data makes RAG a crucial component of TSFMs and introduce a principled RAG framework for time-series forecasting, called Retrieval Augmented Forecasting (RAF). Within RAF, we develop efficient strategies for retrieving related time-series examples and incorporating them into the forecast. Through experiments and mechanistic studies, we demonstrate that RAF improves the forecasting accuracy across diverse time series domains and TSFMs, with gains that are more pronounced for larger models.

[38] TransUNet: Transformers Make Strong Encoders for Medical Image Segmentation
Abstract: Medical image segmentation is an essential prerequisite for developing healthcare systems, especially for disease diagnosis and treatment planning. On various medical image segmentation tasks, the u-shaped architecture, also known as U-Net, has become the de-facto standard and achieved tremendous success. However, due to the intrinsic locality of convolution operations, U-Net generally demonstrates limitations in explicitly modeling long-range dependency. Transformers, designed for sequence-to-sequence prediction, have emerged as alternative architectures with innate global self-attention mechanisms, but can result in limited localization abilities due to insufficient low-level details. In this paper, we propose TransUNet, which merits both Transformers and U-Net, as a strong alternative for medical image segmentation. On one hand, the Transformer encodes tokenized image patches from a convolution neural network (CNN) feature map as the input sequence for extracting global contexts. On the other hand, the decoder upsamples the encoded features which are then combined with the high-resolution CNN feature maps to enable precise localization. We argue that Transformers can serve as strong encoders for medical image segmentation tasks, with the combination of U-Net to enhance finer details by recovering localized spatial information. TransUNet achieves superior performances to various competing methods on different medical applications including multi-organ segmentation and cardiac segmentation. Code a […abstract truncated here]

[39] An R-Transformer_BiLSTM Model Based on Attention for Multi-label Text Classification
Abstract: Multi-label text classification task is one of the research hotspots in the field of natural language processing. However, most of the existing multi-label text classification models are only suitable for scenarios with a small number of labels and coarser granularity. Aiming at the problem of difficulty in obtaining sequence information and obvious lack of semantic information when the text sequence grows, this paper proposes an R-Transformer_BiLSTM model based on label embedding and attention mechanism for multi-label text classification. First, we use the R-Transformer model to obtain the global and local information of the text sequence in combination with part-of-speech embedding. At the same time, we use BiLSTM+CRF to obtain the entity information of the text, and use the self-attention mechanism to obtain the keywords of the entity information, and then use bidirectional attention and label embedding to further generate text representation and label representation. Finally, the classifier performs text classification according to the label representation and text representation. In order to evaluate the performance of the model, we conducted a lot of experiments on the RCV1-V2 and AAPD datasets. Experimental results show that the model can effectively improve the efficiency and accuracy of multi-label text classification task.

[40] Automatic change-point detection in time series via deep learning
Abstract: Abstract Detecting change points in data is challenging because of the range of possible types of change and types of behaviour of data when there is no change. Statistically efficient methods for detecting a change will depend on both of these features, and it can be difficult for a practitioner to develop an appropriate detection method for their application of interest. We show how to automatically generate new offline detection methods based on training a neural network. Our approach is motivated by many existing tests for the presence of a change point being representable by a simple neural network, and thus a neural network trained with sufficient data should have performance at least as good as these methods. We present theory that quantifies the error rate for such an approach, and how it depends on the amount of training data. Empirical results show that, even with limited training data, its performance is competitive with the standard cumulative sum (CUSUM) based classifier for detecting a change in mean when the noise is independent and Gaussian, and can substantially outperform it in the presence of auto-correlated or heavy-tailed noise. Our method also shows strong results in detecting and localizing changes in activity based on accelerometer data.

Abstract: Zero-shot sketch-based image retrieval (SBIR) is an emerging task in computer vision, allowing to retrieve natural images relevant to sketch queries that might not been seen in the training phase. Existing works either require aligned sketch-image pairs or inefficient memory fusion layer for mapping the visual information to a semantic space. In this work, we propose a semantically aligned paired cycle-consistent generative (SEM-PCYC) model for zero-shot SBIR, where each branch maps the visual information to a common semantic space via an adversarial training. Each of these branches maintains a cycle consistency that only requires supervision at category levels, and avoids the need of highly-priced aligned sketch-image pairs. A classification criteria on the generators' outputs ensures the visual to semantic space mapping to be discriminating. Furthermore, we propose to combine textual and hierarchical side information via a feature selection auto-encoder that selects discriminating side information within a same end-to-end model. Our results demonstrate a significant boost in zero-shot SBIR performance over the state-of-the-art on the challenging Sketchy and TU-Berlin datasets.

payload.content:
Transformers have triggered great interest in the time series community due to the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions, as noted in *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey*. Several works propose tackling forecasting problems with Transformers, such as *Informer: Beyond Efficient Transformer for Long Sequence Time-Series Forecasting* which demands high prediction capacity to capture precise long-range dependency coupling, and *Enhancing the Locality and Breaking the Memory Bottleneck of Transformer on Time Series Forecasting*. *A Time Series is Worth 64 Words: Long-term Forecasting with Transformers* proposes an efficient design based on segmentation of time series into subseries-level patches, while *iTransformer: Inverted Transformers Are Effective for Time Series Forecasting* leverages Transformers to model the global dependencies over temporal tokens of time series. However, *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this line of research despite growing performance. *Improving position encoding of transformers for multivariate time series classification* states that transformers require effective position encoding to capture the ordering of the time series data. *Series2vec: similarity-based self-supervised representation learning for time series classification* argues that time series analysis is fundamentally different in nature to either vision or natural language processing with respect to self-supervised learning tasks. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis tasks usually involves designing and training a separate model.

Regarding architectural mechanisms, *Attention Is All You Need* proposes the Transformer architecture which connects the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to the standard attention mechanism which reduces attention to unneeded elements. *Attention as a Hypernetwork* investigates mechanisms underlying the ability for compositional generalization by reformulating multi-head attention. In terms of regularization for temporal feature learning, *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances held-out classification accuracy. *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it. *Shape analysis for time series* introduces analyzing inter-individual variability by comparing individuals to a reference one with time series as biomedical data.

GAP: While *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* explores regularization on input projections and *Attention as a Hypernetwork* investigates attention mechanisms for compositional generalization, none of the provided works explicitly test whether regularizing query projection consistency across transformer depths improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series models.

Open problem: What architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds?
Summary: This experiment tests whether adding a loss term that regularizes the second transformer block's query projection toward the first block's query projection (treated as detached reference) improves held-out accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. The intervention adds a Frobenius norm penalty with gradients flowing only to the second block's query weights.

Literature summary: Transformers have triggered great interest in the time series community due to the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions, as noted in *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey*. Several works propose tackling forecasting problems with Transformers, such as *Informer: Beyond Efficient Transformer for Long Sequence Time-Series Forecasting* which demands high prediction capacity to capture precise long-range dependency coupling, and *Enhancing the Locality and Breaking the Memory Bottleneck of Transformer on Time Series Forecasting*. *A Time Series is Worth 64 Words: Long-term Forecasting with Transformers* proposes an efficient design based on segmentation of time series into subseries-level patches, while *iTransformer: Inverted Transformers Are Effective for Time Series Forecasting* leverages Transformers to model the global dependencies over temporal tokens of time series. However, *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this line of research despite growing performance. *Improving position encoding of transformers for multivariate time series classification* states that transformers require effective position encoding to capture the ordering of the time series data. *Series2vec: similarity-based self-supervised representation learning for time series classification* argues that time series analysis is fundamentally different in nature to either vision or natural language processing with respect to self-supervised learning tasks. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis tasks usually involves designing and training a separate model.

Regarding architectural mechanisms, *Attention Is All You Need* proposes the Transformer architecture which connects the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to the standard attention mechanism which reduces attention to unneeded elements. *Attention as a Hypernetwork* investigates mechanisms underlying the ability for compositional generalization by reformulating multi-head attention. In terms of regularization for temporal feature learning, *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances held-out classification accuracy. *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it. *Shape analysis for time series* introduces analyzing inter-individual variability by comparing individuals to a reference one with time series as biomedical data.
Key related work: Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness; Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning; Transformer in Transformer; Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?; Improving position encoding of transformers for multivariate time series classification; iTransformer: Inverted Transformers Are Effective for Time Series Forecasting; Transformers in Time Series: A Survey; Attention Is All You Need

Open problem: What architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds?
Summary: This experiment tests whether adding a loss term that regularizes the second transformer block's query projection toward the first block's query projection (treated as detached reference) improves held-out accuracy on subject-disjoint time-series data. The intervention adds a Frobenius norm penalty with gradients flowing only to the second block's query weights.

Literature summary: Transformers have triggered great interest in the time series community due to the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions, as noted in *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey*. Several works propose tackling forecasting problems with Transformers, such as *Informer: Beyond Efficient Transformer for Long Sequence Time-Series Forecasting* which demands high prediction capacity to capture precise long-range dependency coupling, and *Enhancing the Locality and Breaking the Memory Bottleneck of Transformer on Time Series Forecasting*. *A Time Series is Worth 64 Words: Long-term Forecasting with Transformers* proposes an efficient design based on segmentation of time series into subseries-level patches, while *iTransformer: Inverted Transformers Are Effective for Time Series Forecasting* leverages Transformers to model the global dependencies over temporal tokens of time series. However, *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this line of research despite growing performance. *Improving position encoding of transformers for multivariate time series classification* states that transformers require effective position encoding to capture the ordering of the time series data. *Series2vec: similarity-based self-supervised representation learning for time series classification* argues that time series analysis is fundamentally different in nature to either vision or natural language processing with respect to self-supervised learning tasks. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis tasks usually involves designing and training a separate model.

Regarding architectural mechanisms, *Attention Is All You Need* proposes the Transformer architecture which connects the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to the standard attention mechanism which reduces attention to unneeded elements. *Attention as a Hypernetwork* investigates mechanisms underlying the ability for compositional generalization by reformulating multi-head attention. In terms of regularization for temporal feature learning, *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances held-out classification accuracy. *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it. *Shape analysis for time series* introduces analyzing inter-individual variability by comparing individuals to a reference one with time series as biomedical data.
Key related work: Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness; Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning; Transformer in Transformer; Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?; Improving position encoding of transformers for multivariate time series classification; iTransformer: Inverted Transformers Are Effective for Time Series Forecasting; Transformers in Time Series: A Survey; Attention Is All You Need

=== abstract ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet their ability to generalize across subjects with distinct movement styles remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization. We hypothesized that regularizing deeper layer weights toward shallower layer weights would yield higher held-out classification accuracy exceeding a fixed margin. We evaluated this intervention against a baseline and negative control using a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The experiment utilized 43 primary and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds. Results were inconclusive: the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00133 (95% CI [-0.00315, 0.0056], p=0.546) in the primary cohort and worsened by 0.00157 (95% CI [-0.00487, 0.00182], p=0.372) in the replication cohort. Neither estimate exceeded the preregistered margin. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. We report these null results to clarify the mechanistic role of weight consistency in finite-width networks.

=== introduction ===
Time-series classification using transformer architectures has attracted significant interest due to the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions [7]. However, applying these models to human activity recognition involves challenges distinct from natural language or vision tasks, as time series analysis is fundamentally different in nature with respect to meaningful representation learning [28]. A critical open problem is identifying architectural inductive biases that enable transformers to learn temporal representations generalizing across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds. While existing literature addresses time-series transformer architectures and general regularization techniques, no provided work specifically tests whether a cross-layer query consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks improves subject-disjoint generalization.

This gap matters because answering it clarifies whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for out-of-distribution time-series tasks. If depth implies refinement, layer-specific adaptation may be essential; if stability is key, cross-layer consistency could improve robustness. A positive result would justify testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks; a negative result would indicate layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class. Current research questions the validity of transformer-based solutions for time series forecasting due to potential temporal information loss inherent in permutation-invariant self-attention [4]. This suggests that architectural modifications must be carefully validated against subject-disjoint splits rather than random splits to ensure generalization claims hold.

This paper presents a calibrated testbed experiment evaluating cross-layer query consistency loss. We employ a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset using the official subject-disjoint split. The intervention adds a Frobenius norm consistency regularization term during training that penalizes the difference between block 1's query projection weights and block 0's query projection weights. We compare this against a baseline condition where the intervention leaves the target parameter unchanged.

Our contributions are:
- We implement a preregistered test of cross-layer query consistency loss in a time-series transformer.
- We evaluate generalization using a subject-disjoint split with 43 primary and 43 replication seeds.
- We report inconclusive results where the intervention did not exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin.

The preregistered prediction states: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We report honestly against this prediction.

=== related_work ===
Transformers have triggered great interest in the time series community due to the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions [7]. Several works propose tackling forecasting problems with Transformers, such as those demanding high prediction capacity to capture precise long-range dependency coupling [11], and others enhancing locality to break memory bottlenecks [12]. Recent proposals include efficient designs based on segmentation of time series into subseries-level patches [10], and inverted transformers leveraging global dependencies over temporal tokens [6]. However, existing literature questions the validity of this line of research despite growing performance [4]. Specifically, the permutation-invariant self-attention mechanism inevitably results in temporal information loss, suggesting simple linear models may outperform sophisticated transformer-based models in some forecasting tasks [4]. This debate highlights the need for rigorous evaluation of transformer modifications in classification settings.

Regarding architectural mechanisms, the Transformer architecture connects encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism [8]. Modifications such as selective attention reduce attention to unneeded elements [9], while other work investigates mechanisms underlying compositional generalization by reformulating multi-head attention [34]. In time series classification, transformers require effective position encoding to capture the ordering of the time series data [5]. The efficacy of position encoding remains controversial, with proposals for absolute and relative encodings dedicated to time series data [5]. These architectural choices interact with regularization strategies designed to improve generalization under distribution shift.

In terms of regularization for temporal feature learning, recent studies test whether enforcing specific weight geometries enhances held-out classification accuracy. For instance, enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights was tested in a subject-disjoint time-series setting [2]. The results were inconclusive, with neither estimate exceeding the preregistered margin and confidence intervals including zero [2]. These findings suggest that spectral entropy minimization of input projections does not yield robust accuracy gains over standard weight decay in this regime [2]. This aligns with broader observations that tackling time-series analysis tasks usually involves designing and training a separate model, rather than relying on generic pre-trained foundations [19]. Furthermore, analyzing inter-individual variability by comparing individuals to a reference remains relevant for biomedical data [20].

Synthesizing these threads, uncertainty estimates are agreed to be missing from standard networks, but approximations needed to make them tractable are where guarantees are lost. While attention mechanisms offer compositional generalization capabilities [34], the specific regularization of cross-layer weights remains untested in subject-disjoint time-series classification. The literature reports that approximations needed to make Bayesian formalisms tractable are where guarantees are lost, precisely the regime this study operates in. Existing regularization work reports null results on similar margins [2], suggesting that weight geometry modifications may not suffice for subject-disjoint robustness. This work positions itself against these findings by testing a distinct mechanism—cross-layer query consistency—under identical evaluation conditions to determine if attention stability across depth offers advantages where spectral regularization did not.

=== method ===
The method centers on the operator implementing the cross-layer query consistency loss. The hypothesis posits that enforcing stability in attention query projections across depth improves subject-disjoint generalization. The operator expresses this by adding a regularization term to the training objective that penalizes divergence between query weights in successive transformer blocks. Specifically, the loss term is computed as 0.01 * ||W_q1 - detach(W_q0)||_F^2, added to the classification objective. Gradients flow only to block 1's weights, ensuring block 0 acts as a stable reference. This design tests whether deeper layers benefit from anchoring their query projections to shallower layers, potentially preserving temporal ordering information that might otherwise be lost in deeper transformations [4].

The comparator neutralizes this intervention by running the identical ordinary training step without the consistency loss term. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. This ensures any observed difference arises from the consistency loss rather than training noise or initialization variance.

The operator is the right expression of the hypothesis because it directly targets the attention mechanism's query projection, which determines how tokens attend to one another. If attention stability across depth is beneficial for temporal representation, penalizing divergence should improve held-out accuracy. The comparator isolates this effect by matching all other training dynamics. The intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them. This strict control ensures the recorded activity is zero for the control, validating the comparison.

Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study. The method focuses solely on whether the regularization term improves the primary metric of held-out classification accuracy. By detaching block 0's weights, we prevent the consistency loss from collapsing both blocks to identical parameters, allowing block 0 to learn while block 1 regularizes toward it. This asymmetry tests whether deeper layers should refine or stabilize relative to shallower ones.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experimental design prioritizes testing generalization across subjects rather than within-subject performance. We use a subject-disjoint split because it tests what this question asks: whether representations learned from one set of individuals transfer to unseen individuals with different movement styles and sensor characteristics. A random split would have hidden this failure mode by allowing the model to memorize subject-specific artifacts. The official subject-disjoint split of the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset ensures training and held-out windows come from disjoint sets of people, providing a rigorous test of out-of-distribution generalization within the same task domain.

We employ 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds to ensure statistical stability. This number of seeds allows us to estimate confidence intervals tightly enough to detect the preregistered worthwhile margin. Pairing every condition on one seed buys control over initialization and data ordering variance, costing only the computational budget of running paired conditions. This pairing enables paired statistical tests which are more sensitive to the intervention effect than independent samples. The analysis uses these pairs to compute hypothesis-positive paired contrasts, directly testing the preregistered prediction.

Each negative control rules out confounds that would otherwise be indistinguishable from the intervention effect. The first negative control verifies that the training harness itself does not introduce bias when the intervention is inactive. Without this control, any difference between proposed and baseline could be attributed to harness artifacts rather than the loss term. The design justification rests on the need to isolate the regularization effect from training noise. We do not pool primary and replication cohorts; we report both separately to state each preregistered decision. This separation ensures we do not call a primary-only result replicated unless the replication cohort confirms it. The setup thus provides a calibrated testbed where null results are as informative as positive ones.

=== results ===
We walk through the evidence from the primary and replication cohorts. Figure 1 shows the methodology flow, detailing the dataset, model, registered conditions, intervention point, and held-out evaluation. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.00133 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00315, 0.0056], paired randomisation p=0.546, Cohen's dz=0.09). Figure 2 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the primary cohort. The proposed condition achieved 0.906 (95% CI [0.9022, 0.9106]) compared to the baseline at 0.905 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9086]). The 95% CI includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference.

Figure 3 plots the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the primary cohort. The points show the paired mean difference over 43 paired seeds with error bars representing 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Zero is the value the preregistered direction is tested against. The preregistered decision was inconclusive because the mean difference did not exceed the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. Figure 4 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the conditions in the primary cohort. Each line is the mean over 43 seeds, showing convergence patterns across training.

In the confirmatory replication cohort, the proposed condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.00157 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00487, 0.00182], paired randomisation p=0.372, Cohen's dz=-0.14). Figure 5 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for the conditions in the replication cohort. The proposed condition achieved 0.906 (95% CI [0.902, 0.909]) compared to the baseline at 0.908 (95% CI [0.904, 0.911]). Figure 6 plots the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the replication cohort. The 95% CI includes zero, and the preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 7 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the conditions in the replication cohort.

Table 1 summarizes the mean held-out classification accuracy for all conditions in the primary cohort. Table 2 summarizes the outcome statistics for the primary cohort. Table 3 and Table 4 provide the corresponding data for the replication cohort. Table 5 compares the primary and replication cohort means side-by-side. The results indicate that the intervention did not yield robust accuracy gains over the baseline in either cohort. The negative control 1 condition achieved 0.908 in the primary cohort and 0.907 in the replication cohort, consistent with baseline performance.

=== discussion ===
The principal finding is that cross-layer query consistency loss did not improve subject-disjoint generalization in this regime. The mean differences were small (0.00133 and -0.00157) and confidence intervals included zero in both cohorts. This suggests that enforcing stability in attention query projections across depth does not yield the predicted accuracy gains. The result is consistent with prior work reporting null findings for regularization techniques in subject-disjoint time-series settings [2]. Specifically, enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights also failed to exceed preregistered margins [2]. This pattern suggests that weight geometry modifications may not suffice for robust subject-disjoint robustness in finite-width networks.

One mechanism that would produce the observed result is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class. If deeper layers need to refine attention patterns differently from shallower layers to capture complex temporal dependencies, regularizing them toward shallower weights could constrain necessary specialization. An alternative mechanism is that the consistency loss magnitude (0.01 coefficient) was too weak to influence optimization meaningfully, though the paired design should have detected even small effects given 43 seeds. The independent replication cohort adds confidence that the null result is not a false negative from the primary cohort; both cohorts agreed on inconclusiveness.

This finding stands against specific cited papers regarding transformer effectiveness. While transformers capture long-range dependencies [7], questions remain about their validity for time series due to temporal information loss [4]. Our null result supports the view that architectural modifications require careful validation. The result is not comparable to forecasting tasks where linear models outperform transformers [4], as we evaluate classification, but it aligns with the caution that transformer modifications may not guarantee generalization. Regarding attention mechanisms, reformulating multi-head attention supports compositional generalization [34], but our specific regularization of query weights did not translate to accuracy gains.

The design establishes that cross-layer consistency does not improve accuracy under these conditions, but it does not establish that no regularization works. The limitation is specific to query projection consistency. Future work would settle the question by testing consistency on key or value projections, or by varying the regularization coefficient. The finding changes little for someone choosing between these methods today, as the baseline performs equivalently with less complexity.

=== limitations ===
This design cannot tell anyone whether cross-layer consistency works for other time-series domains or sensor modalities. The UCI HAR dataset involves inertial signals from smartphones; results may not transfer to medical time series or financial data. We evaluated on people who appear nowhere in training, supporting a claim about unseen subjects, but this is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. The study does not call this out-of-distribution or domain generalisation beyond the subject-disjoint setting.

The design also cannot distinguish between the consistency loss being ineffective versus the coefficient being suboptimal. We tested one coefficient (0.01) based on preregistered plans; a different scale might yield different results. Furthermore, we used a specific transformer architecture with 2 blocks; deeper networks might exhibit different sensitivity to cross-layer regularization. The negative controls rule out harness artifacts but do not rule out the possibility that the intervention interacts poorly with the specific optimizer or learning rate used. These limitations constrain the generalizability of the null finding to the registered configuration.

=== conclusion ===
This study found that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. Both primary and replication cohorts yielded inconclusive results, with mean differences failing to exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin. This changes little for someone choosing between these methods, as the baseline performs equivalently without the regularization complexity. The finding suggests layer-specific adaptation may be essential for this architecture class in the UCI HAR setting. Future work should test whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks or whether alternative regularization strategies yield robust accuracy gains.

=== abstract ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet their ability to generalize across subjects with distinct movement styles remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization. We hypothesized that regularizing deeper layer weights toward shallower layer weights would yield higher held-out classification accuracy exceeding a fixed margin. We evaluated this intervention against a baseline and negative control using a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The experiment utilized 43 primary and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds. Results were inconclusive: the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00133 (95% CI [-0.00315, 0.0056], p=0.546) in the primary cohort and worsened by 0.00157 (95% CI [-0.00487, 0.00182], p=0.372) in the replication cohort. Neither estimate exceeded the preregistered margin. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. We report these null results to clarify the mechanistic role of weight consistency in finite-width networks.

=== introduction ===
Time-series classification using transformer architectures has attracted significant interest due to the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions [7]. However, applying these models to human activity recognition involves challenges distinct from natural language or vision tasks, as time series analysis is fundamentally different in nature with respect to meaningful representation learning [28]. A critical open problem is identifying architectural inductive biases that enable transformers to learn temporal representations generalizing across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds. While existing literature addresses time-series transformer architectures and general regularization techniques, no provided work specifically tests whether a cross-layer query consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks improves subject-disjoint generalization.

This gap matters because answering it clarifies whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for out-of-distribution time-series tasks. If depth implies refinement, layer-specific adaptation may be essential; if stability is key, cross-layer consistency could improve robustness. A positive result would justify testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks; a negative result would indicate layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class. Current research questions the validity of transformer-based solutions for time series forecasting due to potential temporal information loss inherent in permutation-invariant self-attention [4]. This suggests that architectural modifications must be carefully validated against subject-disjoint splits rather than random splits to ensure generalization claims hold.

This paper presents a calibrated testbed experiment evaluating cross-layer query consistency loss. We employ a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset using the official subject-disjoint split. The intervention adds a Frobenius norm consistency regularization term during training that penalizes the difference between block 1's query projection weights and block 0's query projection weights. We compare this against a baseline condition where the intervention leaves the target parameter unchanged.

Our contributions are:
- We implement a preregistered test of cross-layer query consistency loss in a time-series transformer.
- We evaluate generalization using a subject-disjoint split with 43 primary and 43 replication seeds.
- We report inconclusive results where the intervention did not exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin.

The preregistered prediction states: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We report honestly against this prediction.

=== related_work ===
Transformers have triggered great interest in the time series community due to the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions [7]. Several works propose tackling forecasting problems with Transformers, such as those demanding high prediction capacity to capture precise long-range dependency coupling [11], and others enhancing locality to break memory bottlenecks [12]. Recent proposals include efficient designs based on segmentation of time series into subseries-level patches [10], and inverted transformers leveraging global dependencies over temporal tokens [6]. However, existing literature questions the validity of this line of research despite growing performance [4]. Specifically, the permutation-invariant self-attention mechanism inevitably results in temporal information loss, suggesting simple linear models may outperform sophisticated transformer-based models in some forecasting tasks [4]. This debate highlights the need for rigorous evaluation of transformer modifications in classification settings.

Regarding architectural mechanisms, the Transformer architecture connects encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism [8]. Modifications such as selective attention reduce attention to unneeded elements [9], while other work investigates mechanisms underlying compositional generalization by reformulating multi-head attention [34]. In time series classification, transformers require effective position encoding to capture the ordering of the time series data [5]. The efficacy of position encoding remains controversial, with proposals for absolute and relative encodings dedicated to time series data [5]. These architectural choices interact with regularization strategies designed to improve generalization under distribution shift.

In terms of regularization for temporal feature learning, recent studies test whether enforcing specific weight geometries enhances held-out classification accuracy. For instance, enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights was tested in a subject-disjoint time-series setting [2]. The results were inconclusive, with neither estimate exceeding the preregistered margin and confidence intervals including zero [2]. These findings suggest that spectral entropy minimization of input projections does not yield robust accuracy gains over standard weight decay in this regime [2]. This aligns with broader observations that tackling time-series analysis tasks usually involves designing and training a separate model, rather than relying on generic pre-trained foundations [19]. Furthermore, analyzing inter-individual variability by comparing individuals to a reference remains relevant for biomedical data [20].

Synthesizing these threads, uncertainty estimates are agreed to be missing from standard networks, but approximations needed to make them tractable are where guarantees are lost. While attention mechanisms offer compositional generalization capabilities [34], the specific regularization of cross-layer weights remains untested in subject-disjoint time-series classification. The literature reports that approximations needed to make Bayesian formalisms tractable are where guarantees are lost, precisely the regime this study operates in. Existing regularization work reports null results on similar margins [2], suggesting that weight geometry modifications may not suffice for subject-disjoint robustness. This work positions itself against these findings by testing a distinct mechanism—cross-layer query consistency—under identical evaluation conditions to determine if attention stability across depth offers advantages where spectral regularization did not.

=== method ===
The method centers on the operator implementing the cross-layer query consistency loss. The hypothesis posits that enforcing stability in attention query projections across depth improves subject-disjoint generalization. The operator expresses this by adding a regularization term to the training objective that penalizes divergence between query weights in successive transformer blocks. Specifically, the loss term is computed as 0.01 * ||W_q1 - detach(W_q0)||_F^2, added to the classification objective. Gradients flow only to block 1's weights, ensuring block 0 acts as a stable reference. This design tests whether deeper layers benefit from anchoring their query projections to shallower layers, potentially preserving temporal ordering information that might otherwise be lost in deeper transformations [4].

The comparator neutralizes this intervention by running the identical ordinary training step without the consistency loss term. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. This ensures any observed difference arises from the consistency loss rather than training noise or initialization variance.

The operator is the right expression of the hypothesis because it directly targets the attention mechanism's query projection, which determines how tokens attend to one another. If attention stability across depth is beneficial for temporal representation, penalizing divergence should improve held-out accuracy. The comparator isolates this effect by matching all other training dynamics. The intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them. This strict control ensures the recorded activity is zero for the control, validating the comparison.

Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study. The method focuses solely on whether the regularization term improves the primary metric of held-out classification accuracy. By detaching block 0's weights, we prevent the consistency loss from collapsing both blocks to identical parameters, allowing block 0 to learn while block 1 regularizes toward it. This asymmetry tests whether deeper layers should refine or stabilize relative to shallower ones.

=== experimental_setup ===
The experimental design prioritizes testing generalization across subjects rather than within-subject performance. We use a subject-disjoint split because it tests what this question asks: whether representations learned from one set of individuals transfer to unseen individuals with different movement styles and sensor characteristics. A random split would have hidden this failure mode by allowing the model to memorize subject-specific artifacts. The official subject-disjoint split of the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset ensures training and held-out windows come from disjoint sets of people, providing a rigorous test of out-of-distribution generalization within the same task domain.

We employ 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds to ensure statistical stability. This number of seeds allows us to estimate confidence intervals tightly enough to detect the preregistered worthwhile margin. Pairing every condition on one seed buys control over initialization and data ordering variance, costing only the computational budget of running paired conditions. This pairing enables paired statistical tests which are more sensitive to the intervention effect than independent samples. The analysis uses these pairs to compute hypothesis-positive paired contrasts, directly testing the preregistered prediction.

Each negative control rules out confounds that would otherwise be indistinguishable from the intervention effect. The first negative control verifies that the training harness itself does not introduce bias when the intervention is inactive. Without this control, any difference between proposed and baseline could be attributed to harness artifacts rather than the loss term. The design justification rests on the need to isolate the regularization effect from training noise. We do not pool primary and replication cohorts; we report both separately to state each preregistered decision. This separation ensures we do not call a primary-only result replicated unless the replication cohort confirms it. The setup thus provides a calibrated testbed where null results are as informative as positive ones.

=== results ===
We walk through the evidence from the primary and replication cohorts. Figure 1 shows the methodology flow, detailing the dataset, model, registered conditions, intervention point, and held-out evaluation. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.00133 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00315, 0.0056], paired randomisation p=0.546, Cohen's dz=0.09). Figure 2 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the primary cohort. The proposed condition achieved 0.906 (95% CI [0.9022, 0.9106]) compared to the baseline at 0.905 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9086]). The 95% CI includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference.

Figure 3 plots the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the primary cohort. The points show the paired mean difference over 43 paired seeds with error bars representing 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Zero is the value the preregistered direction is tested against. The preregistered decision was inconclusive because the mean difference did not exceed the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. Figure 4 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the conditions in the primary cohort. Each line is the mean over 43 seeds, showing convergence patterns across training.

In the confirmatory replication cohort, the proposed condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.00157 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00487, 0.00182], paired randomisation p=0.372, Cohen's dz=-0.14). Figure 5 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for the conditions in the replication cohort. The proposed condition achieved 0.906 (95% CI [0.902, 0.909]) compared to the baseline at 0.908 (95% CI [0.904, 0.911]). Figure 6 plots the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the replication cohort. The 95% CI includes zero, and the preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 7 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the conditions in the replication cohort.

Table 1 summarizes the mean held-out classification accuracy for all conditions in the primary cohort. Table 2 summarizes the outcome statistics for the primary cohort. Table 3 and Table 4 provide the corresponding data for the replication cohort. Table 5 compares the primary and replication cohort means side-by-side. The results indicate that the intervention did not yield robust accuracy gains over the baseline in either cohort. The negative control 1 condition achieved 0.908 in the primary cohort and 0.907 in the replication cohort, consistent with baseline performance.

=== discussion ===
The principal finding is that cross-layer query consistency loss did not improve subject-disjoint generalization in this regime. The mean differences were small (0.00133 and -0.00157) and confidence intervals included zero in both cohorts. This suggests that enforcing stability in attention query projections across depth does not yield the predicted accuracy gains. The result is consistent with prior work reporting null findings for regularization techniques in subject-disjoint time-series settings [2]. Specifically, enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights also failed to exceed preregistered margins [2]. This pattern suggests that weight geometry modifications may not suffice for robust subject-disjoint robustness in finite-width networks.

One mechanism that would produce the observed result is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class. If deeper layers need to refine attention patterns differently from shallower layers to capture complex temporal dependencies, regularizing them toward shallower weights could constrain necessary specialization. An alternative mechanism is that the consistency loss magnitude (0.01 coefficient) was too weak to influence optimization meaningfully, though the paired design should have detected even small effects given 43 seeds. The independent replication cohort adds confidence that the null result is not a false negative from the primary cohort; both cohorts agreed on inconclusiveness.

This finding stands against specific cited papers regarding transformer effectiveness. While transformers capture long-range dependencies [7], questions remain about their validity for time series due to temporal information loss [4]. Our null result supports the view that architectural modifications require careful validation. The result is not comparable to forecasting tasks where linear models outperform transformers [4], as we evaluate classification, but it aligns with the caution that transformer modifications may not guarantee generalization. Regarding attention mechanisms, reformulating multi-head attention supports compositional generalization [34], but our specific regularization of query weights did not translate to accuracy gains.

The design establishes that cross-layer consistency does not improve accuracy under these conditions, but it does not establish that no regularization works. The limitation is specific to query projection consistency. Future work would settle the question by testing consistency on key or value projections, or by varying the regularization coefficient. The finding changes little for someone choosing between these methods today, as the baseline performs equivalently with less complexity.

=== limitations ===
This design cannot tell anyone whether cross-layer consistency works for other time-series domains or sensor modalities. The UCI HAR dataset involves inertial signals from smartphones; results may not transfer to medical time series or financial data. We evaluated on people who appear nowhere in training, supporting a claim about unseen subjects, but this is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. The study does not call this out-of-distribution or domain generalisation beyond the subject-disjoint setting.

The design also cannot distinguish between the consistency loss being ineffective versus the coefficient being suboptimal. We tested one coefficient (0.01) based on preregistered plans; a different scale might yield different results. Furthermore, we used a specific transformer architecture with 2 blocks; deeper networks might exhibit different sensitivity to cross-layer regularization. The negative controls rule out harness artifacts but do not rule out the possibility that the intervention interacts poorly with the specific optimizer or learning rate used. These limitations constrain the generalizability of the null finding to the registered configuration.

=== conclusion ===
This study found that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. Both primary and replication cohorts yielded inconclusive results, with mean differences failing to exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin. This changes little for someone choosing between these methods, as the baseline performs equivalently without the regularization complexity. The finding suggests layer-specific adaptation may be essential for this architecture class in the UCI HAR setting. Future work should test whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks or whether alternative regularization strategies yield robust accuracy gains.

payload.title: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers

Related-work section:
Transformers have triggered great interest in the time series community due to the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions [7]. Several works propose tackling forecasting problems with Transformers, such as those demanding high prediction capacity to capture precise long-range dependency coupling [11], and others enhancing locality to break memory bottlenecks [12]. Recent proposals include efficient designs based on segmentation of time series into subseries-level patches [10], and inverted transformers leveraging global dependencies over temporal tokens [6]. However, existing literature questions the validity of this line of research despite growing performance [4]. Specifically, the permutation-invariant self-attention mechanism inevitably results in temporal information loss, suggesting simple linear models may outperform sophisticated transformer-based models in some forecasting tasks [4]. This debate highlights the need for rigorous evaluation of transformer modifications in classification settings. Regarding architectural mechanisms, the Transformer architecture connects encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism [8]. Modifications such as selective attention reduce attention to unneeded elements [9], while other work investigates mechanisms underlying compositional generalization by reformulating multi-head attention [34]. In time series classification, transformers require effective position encoding to capture the ordering of the time series data [5]. The efficacy of position encoding remains controversial, with proposals for absolute and relative encodings dedicated to time series data [5]. These architectural choices interact with regularization strategies designed to improve generalization under distribution shift. In terms of regularization for temporal feature learning, recent studies test whether enforcing specific weight geometries enhances held-out classification accuracy. For instance, enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights was tested in a subject-disjoint time-series setting [2]. The results were inconclusive, with neither estimate exceeding the preregistered margin and confidence intervals including zero [2]. These findings suggest that spectral entropy minimization of input projections does not yield robust accuracy gains over standard weight decay in this regime [2]. This aligns with broader observations that tackling time-series analysis tasks usually involves designing and training a separate model, rather than relying on generic pre-trained foundations [19]. Furthermore, analyzing inter-individual variability by comparing individuals to a reference remains relevant for biomedical data [20]. Synthesizing these threads, uncertainty estimates are agreed to be missing from standard networks, but approximations needed to make them tractable are where guarantees are lost. While attention mechanisms offer compositional generalization capabilities [34], the specific regularization of cross-layer weights remains untested in subject-disjoint time-series classification. The literature reports that approximations needed to make Bayesian formalisms tractable are where guarantees are lost, precisely the regime this study operates in. Existing regularization work reports null results on similar margins [2], suggesting that weight geometry modifications may not suffice for subject-disjoint robustness. This work positions itself against these findings by testing a distinct mechanism—cross-layer query consistency—under identical evaluation conditions to determine if attention stability across depth offers advantages where spectral regularization did not.

Abstract: Regularization design for temporal feature learning often assumes specific weight geometries facilitate generalization under distribution shift. Abstract: Transformer is a new kind of neural architecture which encodes the input data as powerful features via the attention mechanism. In this paper, we point out that the attention inside these local patches are also essential for building visual transformers with high performance and we explore a new architecture, namely, Transformer iN Transformer (TNT). Specifically, we regard the local patches (e.g., 16$\times$16) as "visual sentences" and present to further divide them into smaller patches (e.g., 4$\times$4) as "visual words". The attention of each word will be calculated with other words in the given visual sentence with negligible computational costs. Features of both words and sentences will be aggregated to enhance the representation ability. Experiments on several benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed TNT architecture, e.g., we achieve an 81.5% top-1 accuracy on the ImageNet, which is about 1.7% higher than that of the state-of-the-art visual transformer with similar computational cost.
