[37] Retrieval Augmented Time Series Forecasting
Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a central component of modern LLM systems, particularly in scenarios where up-to-date information is crucial for accurately responding to user queries or when queries exceed the scope of the training data. The advent of time-series foundation models (TSFM), such as Chronos or Moirai, and the need for effective zero-shot forecasting performance across various time-series domains motivates the question: Do the benefits of RAG similarly carry over to time series forecasting? In this paper, we advocate that the dynamic and event-driven nature of time-series data makes RAG a crucial component of TSFMs and introduce a principled RAG framework for time-series forecasting, called Retrieval Augmented Forecasting (RAF). Within RAF, we develop efficient strategies for retrieving related time-series examples and incorporating them into the forecast. Through experiments and mechanistic studies, we demonstrate that RAF improves the forecasting accuracy across diverse time series domains and TSFMs, with gains that are more pronounced for larger models.

[38] TransUNet: Transformers Make Strong Encoders for Medical Image Segmentation
Abstract: Medical image segmentation is an essential prerequisite for developing healthcare systems, especially for disease diagnosis and treatment planning. On various medical image segmentation tasks, the u-shaped architecture, also known as U-Net, has become the de-facto standard and achieved tremendous success. However, due to the intrinsic locality of convolution operations, U-Net generally demonstrates limitations in explicitly modeling long-range dependency. Transformers, designed for sequence-to-sequence prediction, have emerged as alternative architectures with innate global self-attention mechanisms, but can result in limited localization abilities due to insufficient low-level details. In this paper, we propose TransUNet, which merits both Transformers and U-Net, as a strong alternative for medical image segmentation. On one hand, the Transformer encodes tokenized image patches from a convolution neural network (CNN) feature map as the input sequence for extracting global contexts. On the other hand, the decoder upsamples the encoded features which are then combined with the high-resolution CNN feature maps to enable precise localization. We argue that Transformers can serve as strong encoders for medical image segmentation tasks, with the combination of U-Net to enhance finer details by recovering localized spatial information. TransUNet achieves superior performances to various competing methods on different medical applications including multi-organ segmentation and cardiac segmentation. Code a […abstract truncated here]

[39] An R-Transformer_BiLSTM Model Based on Attention for Multi-label Text Classification
Abstract: Multi-label text classification task is one of the research hotspots in the field of natural language processing. However, most of the existing multi-label text classification models are only suitable for scenarios with a small number of labels and coarser granularity. Aiming at the problem of difficulty in obtaining sequence information and obvious lack of semantic information when the text sequence grows, this paper proposes an R-Transformer_BiLSTM model based on label embedding and attention mechanism for multi-label text classification. First, we use the R-Transformer model to obtain the global and local information of the text sequence in combination with part-of-speech embedding. At the same time, we use BiLSTM+CRF to obtain the entity information of the text, and use the self-attention mechanism to obtain the keywords of the entity information, and then use bidirectional attention and label embedding to further generate text representation and label representation. Finally, the classifier performs text classification according to the label representation and text representation. In order to evaluate the performance of the model, we conducted a lot of experiments on the RCV1-V2 and AAPD datasets. Experimental results show that the model can effectively improve the efficiency and accuracy of multi-label text classification task.

[40] Automatic change-point detection in time series via deep learning
Abstract: Abstract Detecting change points in data is challenging because of the range of possible types of change and types of behaviour of data when there is no change. Statistically efficient methods for detecting a change will depend on both of these features, and it can be difficult for a practitioner to develop an appropriate detection method for their application of interest. We show how to automatically generate new offline detection methods based on training a neural network. Our approach is motivated by many existing tests for the presence of a change point being representable by a simple neural network, and thus a neural network trained with sufficient data should have performance at least as good as these methods. We present theory that quantifies the error rate for such an approach, and how it depends on the amount of training data. Empirical results show that, even with limited training data, its performance is competitive with the standard cumulative sum (CUSUM) based classifier for detecting a change in mean when the noise is independent and Gaussian, and can substantially outperform it in the presence of auto-correlated or heavy-tailed noise. Our method also shows strong results in detecting and localizing changes in activity based on accelerometer data.

[41] Semantically Tied Paired Cycle Consistency for Zero-Shot Sketch-Based Image Retrieval
Abstract: Zero-shot sketch-based image retrieval (SBIR) is an emerging task in computer vision, allowing to retrieve natural images relevant to sketch queries that might not been seen in the training phase. Existing works either require aligned sketch-image pairs or inefficient memory fusion layer for mapping the visual information to a semantic space. In this work, we propose a semantically aligned paired cycle-consistent generative (SEM-PCYC) model for zero-shot SBIR, where each branch maps the visual information to a common semantic space via an adversarial training. Each of these branches maintains a cycle consistency that only requires supervision at category levels, and avoids the need of highly-priced aligned sketch-image pairs. A classification criteria on the generators' outputs ensures the visual to semantic space mapping to be discriminating. Furthermore, we propose to combine textual and hierarchical side information via a feature selection auto-encoder that selects discriminating side information within a same end-to-end model. Our results demonstrate a significant boost in zero-shot SBIR performance over the state-of-the-art on the challenging Sketchy and TU-Berlin datasets.

Abstract: Hyperspectral images’ (HSIs) classification research has seen significant progress with the use of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and Transformer blocks. However, these studies primarily incorporated Transformer blocks at the end of their network architectures. Due to significant differences between the spectral and spatial features in HSIs, the extraction of both global and local spectral–spatial features remains incomplete. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a novel method called TransHSI. This method incorporates a new spectral–spatial feature extraction module that leverages 3D CNNs to fuse Transformer to extract the local and global spectral features of HSIs, then combining 2D CNNs and Transformer to capture the local and global spatial features of HSIs comprehensively. Furthermore, a fusion module is proposed, which not only integrates the learned shallow and deep features of HSIs but also applies a semantic tokenizer to transform the fused features, enhancing the discriminative power of the features. This paper conducts experiments on three public datasets: Indian Pines, Pavia University, and Data Fusion Contest 2018. The training and test sets are selected based on a disjoint sampling strategy. We perform a comparative analysis with 11 traditional and advanced HSI classification algorithms. FINISHED PAPER:
Abstract: Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet their ability to generalize across subjects with distinct movement styles remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization. We hypothesized that regularizing deeper layer weights toward shallower layer weights would yield higher held-out classification accuracy exceeding a fixed margin. We evaluated this intervention against a baseline and negative control using a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The experiment utilized 43 primary and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds. Results were inconclusive: the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00133 (95% CI [-0.00315, 0.0056], p=0.546) in the primary cohort and worsened by 0.00157 (95% CI [-0.00487, 0.00182], p=0.372) in the replication cohort. Neither estimate exceeded the preregistered margin. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. We report these null results to clarify the mechanistic role of weight consistency in finite-width networks.

Introduction: Time-series classification using transformer architectures has attracted significant interest due to the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions [7]. However, applying these models to human activity recognition involves challenges distinct from natural language or vision tasks, as time series analysis is fundamentally different in nature with respect to meaningful representation learning [28]. A critical open problem is identifying architectural inductive biases that enable transformers to learn temporal representations generalizing across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds. While existing literature addresses time-series transformer architectures and general regularization techniques, no provided work specifically tests whether a cross-layer query consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks improves subject-disjoint generalization. This gap matters because answering it clarifies whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for out-of-distribution time-series tasks. If depth implies refinement, layer-specific adaptation may be essential; if stability is key, cross-layer consistency could improve robustness. A positive result would justify testing whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks; a negative result would indicate layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class. Current research questions the validity of transformer-based solutions for time series forecasting due to potential temporal information loss inherent in permutation-invariant self-attention [4]. This suggests that architectural modifications must be carefully validated against subject-disjoint splits rather than random splits to ensure generalization claims hold. This paper presents a calibrated testbed experiment evaluating cross-layer query consistency loss. We employ a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset using the official subject-disjoint split. The intervention adds a Frobenius norm consistency regularization term during training that penalizes the difference between block 1's query projection weights and block 0's query projection weights. We compare this against a baseline condition where the intervention leaves the target parameter unchanged. Our contributions are:
- We implement a preregistered test of cross-layer query consistency loss in a time-series transformer. - We evaluate generalization using a subject-disjoint split with 43 primary and 43 replication seeds. - We report inconclusive results where the intervention did not exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin. The preregistered prediction states: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean paired contrast in the hypothesised direction H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

Discussion: The principal finding is that cross-layer query consistency loss did not improve subject-disjoint generalization in this regime. The mean differences were small (0.00133 and -0.00157) and confidence intervals included zero in both cohorts. This suggests that enforcing stability in attention query projections across depth does not yield the predicted accuracy gains. The result is consistent with prior work reporting null findings for regularization techniques in subject-disjoint time-series settings [2]. Specifically, enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights also failed to exceed preregistered margins [2]. This pattern suggests that weight geometry modifications may not suffice for robust subject-disjoint robustness in finite-width networks. One mechanism that would produce the observed result is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class. If deeper layers need to refine attention patterns differently from shallower layers to capture complex temporal dependencies, regularizing them toward shallower weights could constrain necessary specialization. An alternative mechanism is that the consistency loss magnitude (0.01 coefficient) was too weak to influence optimization meaningfully, though the paired design should have detected even small effects given 43 seeds. The independent replication cohort adds confidence that the null result is not a false negative from the primary cohort; both cohorts agreed on inconclusiveness. This finding stands against specific cited papers regarding transformer effectiveness. While transformers capture long-range dependencies [7], questions remain about their validity for time series due to temporal information loss [4]. Our null result supports the view that architectural modifications require careful validation. The result is not comparable to forecasting tasks where linear models outperform transformers [4], as we evaluate classification, but it aligns with the caution that transformer modifications may not guarantee generalization. Regarding attention mechanisms, reformulating multi-head attention supports compositional generalization [34], but our specific regularization of query weights did not translate to accuracy gains. The design establishes that cross-layer consistency does not improve accuracy under these conditions, but it does not establish that no regularization works. The limitation is specific to query projection consistency. Future work would settle the question by testing consistency on key or value projections, or by varying the regularization coefficient. The finding changes little for someone choosing between these methods today, as the baseline performs equivalently with less complexity.

Conclusion: This study found that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. Both primary and replication cohorts yielded inconclusive results, with mean differences failing to exceed the preregistered worthwhile margin. This changes little for someone choosing between these methods, as the baseline performs equivalently without the regularization complexity. The finding suggests layer-specific adaptation may be essential for this architecture class in the UCI HAR setting. Future work should test whether cross-layer consistency transfers to other subject-disjoint time-series benchmarks or whether alternative regularization strategies yield robust accuracy gains.

Title: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Abstract: Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet their ability to generalize across subjects with distinct movement styles remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization. We hypothesized that regularizing deeper layer weights toward shallower layer weights would yield higher held-out classification accuracy exceeding a fixed margin. We evaluated this intervention against a baseline and negative control using a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The experiment utilized 43 primary and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds. Results were inconclusive: the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00133 (95% CI [-0.00315, 0.0056], p=0.546) in the primary cohort and worsened by 0.00157 (95% CI [-0.00487, 0.00182], p=0.372) in the replication cohort. Neither estimate exceeded the preregistered margin. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. We report these null results to clarify the mechanistic role of weight consistency in finite-width networks.
Related work: Transformers have triggered great interest in the time series community due to the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions [7]. Several works propose tackling forecasting problems with Transformers, such as those demanding high prediction capacity to capture precise long-range dependency coupling [11], and others enhancing locality to break memory bottlenecks [12]. Recent proposals include efficient designs based on segmentation of time series into subseries-level patches [10], and inverted transformers leveraging global dependencies over temporal tokens [6]. However, existing literature questions the validity of this line of research despite growing performance [4]. Specifically, the permutation-invariant self-attention mechanism inevitably results in temporal information loss, suggesting simple linear models may outperform sophisticated transformer-based models in some forecasting tasks [4]. This debate highlights the need for rigorous evaluation of transformer modifications in classification settings. Regarding architectural mechanisms, the Transformer architecture connects encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism [8]. Modifications such as selective attention reduce attention to unneeded elements [9], while other work investigates mechanisms underlying compositional generalization by reformulating multi-head attention [34]. In time series classification, transformers require effective position encoding to capture the ordering of the time series data [5]. The efficacy of position encoding remains controversial, with proposals for absolute and relative encodings dedicated to time series data [5]. These architectural choices interact with regularization strategies designed to improve generalization under distribution shift. In terms of regularization for temporal feature learning, recent studies test whether enforcing specific weight geometries enhances held-out classification accuracy. For instance, enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights was tested in a subject-disjoint time-series setting [2]. The results were inconclusive, with neither estimate exceeding the preregistered margin and confidence intervals including zero [2]. These findings suggest that spectral entropy minimization of input projections does not yield robust accuracy gains over standard weight decay in this regime [2]. This aligns with broader observations that tackling time-series analysis tasks usually involves designing and training a separate model, rather than relying on generic pre-trained foundations [19]. Furthermore, analyzing inter-individual variability by comparing individuals to a reference remains relevant for biomedical data [20]. Synthesizing these threads, uncertainty estimates are agreed to be missing from standard networks, but approximations needed to make them tractable are where guarantees are lost. While attention mechanisms offer compositional generalization capabilities [34], the specific regularization of cross-layer weights remains untested in subject-disjoint time-series classification. The literature reports that approximations needed to make Bayesian formalisms tractable are where guarantees are lost, precisely the regime this study operates in. Existing regularization work reports null results on similar margins [2], suggesting that weight geometry modifications may not suffice for subject-disjoint robustness. This work positions itself against these findings by testing a distinct mechanism—cross-layer query consistency—under identical evaluation conditions to determine if attention stability across depth offers advantages where spectral regularization did not.
Method: The method centers on the operator implementing the cross-layer query consistency loss. The hypothesis posits that enforcing stability in attention query projections across depth improves subject-disjoint generalization. The operator expresses this by adding a regularization term to the training objective that penalizes divergence between query weights in successive transformer blocks. Specifically, the loss term is computed as 0.01 * ||W_q1 - detach(W_q0)||_F^2, added to the classification objective. Gradients flow only to block 1's weights, ensuring block 0 acts as a stable reference. This design tests whether deeper layers benefit from anchoring their query projections to shallower layers, potentially preserving temporal ordering information that might otherwise be lost in deeper transformations [4]. The comparator neutralizes this intervention by running the identical ordinary training step without the consistency loss term. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. This ensures any observed difference arises from the consistency loss rather than training noise or initialization variance. The operator is the right expression of the hypothesis because it directly targets the attention mechanism's query projection, which determines how tokens attend to one another. If attention stability across depth is beneficial for temporal representation, penalizing divergence should improve held-out accuracy. The comparator isolates this effect by matching all other training dynamics. The intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them. This strict control ensures the recorded activity is zero for the control, validating the comparison. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study. The method focuses solely on whether the regularization term improves the primary metric of held-out classification accuracy. By detaching block 0's weights, we prevent the consistency loss from collapsing both blocks to identical parameters, allowing block 0 to learn while block 1 regularizes toward it. This asymmetry tests whether deeper layers should refine or stabilize relative to shallower ones.

Operator specification. CrossLayerQueryConsistency is applied to blocks.1.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents in the training objective from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute in the training objective = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store in the training objective in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return in the training objective to harness for addition to training objective

The following invariants hold throughout:
- Reference weights from block 0 are detached and receive no gradients
- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

Control arm. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. If the condition the harness passes in is a control condition, return here: add no term to the training objective, and leave the registered target parameter and that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer exactly as received. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.
Results: We walk through the evidence from the primary and replication cohorts. Figure 1 shows the methodology flow, detailing the dataset, model, registered conditions, intervention point, and held-out evaluation. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.00133 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00315, 0.0056], paired randomisation p=0.546, Cohen's dz=0.09). Figure 2 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the primary cohort. The proposed condition achieved 0.906 (95% CI [0.9022, 0.9106]) compared to the baseline at 0.905 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9086]). The 95% CI includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. Figure 3 plots the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the primary cohort. The points show the paired mean difference over 43 paired seeds with error bars representing 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Zero is the value the preregistered direction is tested against. The preregistered decision was inconclusive because the mean difference did not exceed the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. Figure 4 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the conditions in the primary cohort. Each line is the mean over 43 seeds, showing convergence patterns across training. In the confirmatory replication cohort, the proposed condition worsened the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.00157 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00487, 0.00182], paired randomisation p=0.372, Cohen's dz=-0.14). Figure 5 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for the conditions in the replication cohort. The proposed condition achieved 0.906 (95% CI [0.902, 0.909]) compared to the baseline at 0.908 (95% CI [0.904, 0.911]). Figure 6 plots the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the replication cohort. The 95% CI includes zero, and the preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 7 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the conditions in the replication cohort. Table 1 summarizes the mean held-out classification accuracy for all conditions in the primary cohort. Table 2 summarizes the outcome statistics for the primary cohort. Table 3 and Table 4 provide the corresponding data for the replication cohort. Table 5 compares the primary and replication cohort means side-by-side. The results indicate that the intervention did not yield robust accuracy gains over the baseline in either cohort. The negative control 1 condition achieved 0.908 in the primary cohort and 0.907 in the replication cohort, consistent with baseline performance. Registered-report decision: the primary cohort was classified as **inconclusive** and the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort, on a disjoint set of seeds, was classified as **inconclusive** under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Discussion: The principal finding is that cross-layer query consistency loss did not improve subject-disjoint generalization in this regime. The mean differences were small (0.00133 and -0.00157) and confidence intervals included zero in both cohorts. This suggests that enforcing stability in attention query projections across depth does not yield the predicted accuracy gains. The result is consistent with prior work reporting null findings for regularization techniques in subject-disjoint time-series settings [2]. Specifically, enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights also failed to exceed preregistered margins [2]. This pattern suggests that weight geometry modifications may not suffice for robust subject-disjoint robustness in finite-width networks. One mechanism that would produce the observed result is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class. If deeper layers need to refine attention patterns differently from shallower layers to capture complex temporal dependencies, regularizing them toward shallower weights could constrain necessary specialization. An alternative mechanism is that the consistency loss magnitude (0.01 coefficient) was too weak to influence optimization meaningfully, though the paired design should have detected even small effects given 43 seeds. The independent replication cohort adds confidence that the null result is not a false negative from the primary cohort; both cohorts agreed on inconclusiveness. This finding stands against specific cited papers regarding transformer effectiveness. While transformers capture long-range dependencies [7], questions remain about their validity for time series due to temporal information loss [4]. Our null result supports the view that architectural modifications require careful validation. The result is not comparable to forecasting tasks where linear models outperform transformers [4], as we evaluate classification, but it aligns with the caution that transformer modifications may not guarantee generalization. Regarding attention mechanisms, reformulating multi-head attention supports compositional generalization [34], but our specific regularization of query weights did not translate to accuracy gains. The design establishes that cross-layer consistency does not improve accuracy under these conditions, but it does not establish that no regularization works. The limitation is specific to query projection consistency. Future work would settle the question by testing consistency on key or value projections, or by varying the regularization coefficient. The finding changes little for someone choosing between these methods today, as the baseline performs equivalently with less complexity.
Limitations: This design cannot tell anyone whether cross-layer consistency works for other time-series domains or sensor modalities. The UCI HAR dataset involves inertial signals from smartphones; results may not transfer to medical time series or financial data. We evaluated on people who appear nowhere in training, supporting a claim about unseen subjects, but this is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. The study does not call this out-of-distribution or domain generalisation beyond the subject-disjoint setting. The design also cannot distinguish between the consistency loss being ineffective versus the coefficient being suboptimal. We tested one coefficient (0.01) based on preregistered plans; a different scale might yield different results. Furthermore, we used a specific transformer architecture with 2 blocks; deeper networks might exhibit different sensitivity to cross-layer regularization. The negative controls rule out harness artifacts but do not rule out the possibility that the intervention interacts poorly with the specific optimizer or learning rate used. These limitations constrain the generalizability of the null finding to the registered configuration. Declared scope. This is a preregistered, single-testbed registered report: every claim in this paper is scoped to the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 and to the preregistered smallest worthwhile effect of 0.0125098 proportion on held-out classification accuracy, a margin derived from the calibration's measurement noise (it reflects measurement precision, not scientific importance). Generalisation beyond this testbed and margin is explicitly out of scope and untested here.

Topic: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Research question: Does enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections, where deeper layer weights are regularized toward shallower layer weights, improve subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers?
Hypothesis: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.
Open problem this targets: What architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds?
Why it matters (impact): Answering this clarifies whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for OOD time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting. Transformers have triggered great interest in the time series community due to the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions, as noted in *Transformers in Time Series: A Survey*. Several works propose tackling forecasting problems with Transformers, such as *Informer: Beyond Efficient Transformer for Long Sequence Time-Series Forecasting* which demands high prediction capacity to capture precise long-range dependency coupling, and *Enhancing the Locality and Breaking the Memory Bottleneck of Transformer on Time Series Forecasting*. *A Time Series is Worth 64 Words: Long-term Forecasting with Transformers* proposes an efficient design based on segmentation of time series into subseries-level patches, while *iTransformer: Inverted Transformers Are Effective for Time Series Forecasting* leverages Transformers to model the global dependencies over temporal tokens of time series. However, *Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?* questions the validity of this line of research despite growing performance. *Improving position encoding of transformers for multivariate time series classification* states that transformers require effective position encoding to capture the ordering of the time series data. *Series2vec: similarity-based self-supervised representation learning for time series classification* argues that time series analysis is fundamentally different in nature to either vision or natural language processing with respect to self-supervised learning tasks. *Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks* observes that tackling time-series analysis tasks usually involves designing and training a separate model.

Regarding architectural mechanisms, *Attention Is All You Need* proposes the Transformer architecture which connects the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism. *Selective Attention Improves Transformer* introduces a parameter-free change to the standard attention mechanism which reduces attention to unneeded elements. *Attention as a Hypernetwork* investigates mechanisms underlying the ability for compositional generalization by reformulating multi-head attention. In terms of regularization for temporal feature learning, *Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning* tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances held-out classification accuracy. *Entropy-Maximized Multiplicative Weight Noise for Subject-Disjoint Robustness* carries a retracted notice from the journal that published it. *Shape analysis for time series* introduces analyzing inter-individual variability by comparing individuals to a reference one with time series as biomedical data.

=== abstract ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet it remains unclear whether architectural depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns to generalize across subjects. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. We implemented a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks within a PreNormTransformerEncoder trained on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset. The experiment utilized an official subject-disjoint split, evaluating held-out classification accuracy across 43 primary seeds and a confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. Results were inconclusive: in the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00133 (95% CI [-0.00315, 0.0056], p=0.546) versus the baseline, and in the replication cohort, it worsened by -0.00157 (95% CI [-0.00487, 0.00182], p=0.372). Neither estimate exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin, and confidence intervals included zero. Variation is attributed to the random seeds that produced each observation, not subjects. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains over standard training in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint tasks.

=== introduction ===
Transformer architectures have triggered great interest in the time-series community due to the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions [7]. While standard transformers were originally designed for sequence transduction tasks in natural language processing [8], their application to temporal data requires careful adaptation to preserve ordering and handle multivariate correlations [5]. A central open problem concerns what architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds. Specifically, it is unknown whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined attention patterns or consistently stable ones to support out-of-distribution generalization in human activity recognition.

Answering this clarifies whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for out-of-distribution time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting. If deeper layers benefit from aligning their query projections with shallower layers, it would suggest that stability across depth is a valuable inductive bias for subject-disjoint generalization. Conversely, if no benefit is observed, it would indicate that layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class. This distinction matters for practitioners choosing between standard training and regularized variants for deployment on unseen subjects.

Existing literature addresses time-series transformer architectures and general regularization techniques, but no provided work specifically tests whether a cross-layer query consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks improves subject-disjoint generalization. While some works propose tackling forecasting problems with transformers by capturing precise long-range dependency coupling [11], others question the validity of this line of research despite growing performance [4]. Regularization design often assumes specific weight geometries facilitate generalization under distribution shift, yet recent studies report inconclusive outcomes for spectral entropy minimization in similar settings [2]. Furthermore, time-series analysis is fundamentally different in nature to either vision or natural language processing with respect to self-supervised learning tasks, suggesting that adaptations successful in other domains may not transfer directly [28].

This paper reports a preregistered experiment testing whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency term penalizing the difference between block query weights, while the baseline maintained identical training dynamics without this term. We evaluated held-out classification accuracy across 43 primary seeds and a confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds.

The contributions of this work are:
- We implement a calibrated testbed for cross-layer query consistency in time-series transformers with subject-disjoint evaluation.
- We report preregistered primary and confirmatory replication results with exact confidence intervals and effect sizes.
- We provide evidence regarding the utility of attention stability across depth for subject-disjoint generalization.

The preregistered prediction was that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== related_work ===
**Transformer Architectures for Time Series**
Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time-series community [7]. Several works propose tackling forecasting problems with transformers, such as those demanding high prediction capacity to capture precise long-range dependency coupling [11]. To address issues like locality-agnostics and memory bottlenecks, researchers have proposed convolutional self-attention and sparse mechanisms to incorporate local context better [12]. Efficient designs based on segmentation of time series into subseries-level patches have also been proposed to retain local semantic information [10]. Inverted transformers apply attention on variate tokens (inverted dimensions) to capture multivariate correlations, contrasting with standard forecasters that model global dependencies over temporal tokens [6]. However, some research questions the validity of this line of research despite growing performance, noting that the permutation-invariant self-attention mechanism inevitably results in temporal information loss [4]. Tackling time-series analysis tasks usually involves designing and training a separate model, which motivates the search for robust architectural inductive biases [19].

**Regularization and Generalization Mechanisms**
Regarding architectural mechanisms, the transformer architecture connects the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism [8]. Selective attention introduces a parameter-free change to the standard attention mechanism which reduces attention to unneeded elements [9]. Mechanisms underlying the ability for compositional generalization have been investigated by reformulating multi-head attention as a hypernetwork [34]. In terms of regularization for temporal feature learning, some studies test whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances held-out classification accuracy [2]. Analyzing inter-individual variability by comparing individuals to a reference one with time series as biomedical data introduces challenges in shape analysis [20]. Transformers require effective position encoding to capture the ordering of the time series data, and the efficacy of position encoding in time-series analysis is not well-studied and remains controversial [5]. Uncertainty estimates are agreed to be missing from standard networks and Bayesian formalisms are the usual answer, but the same literature reports that the approximations needed to make them tractable are where the guarantees are lost — precisely the regime this study operates in.

**Subject-Disjoint Evaluation**
Time-series analysis is fundamentally different in nature to either vision or natural language processing with respect to self-supervised learning tasks [28]. While existing literature addresses time-series transformer architectures and general regularization techniques, no provided work specifically tests whether a cross-layer query consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks improves subject-disjoint generalization. Regularization design for temporal feature learning often assumes specific weight geometries facilitate generalization under distribution shift, yet recent studies report inconclusive outcomes for spectral entropy minimization in similar settings [2]. This gap motivates the current investigation into whether attention stability across depth provides a robust inductive bias for unseen subjects.

=== method ===
The experiment runs the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1. The model is a PreNormTransformerEncoder consisting of a Linear input projection (9 to 64 dimensions) plus a learned positional embedding (128 to 64 dimensions). It contains 2 blocks, each comprising LayerNorm (64), 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with query/key/value/output Linear projections (64 to 64), a residual connection, LayerNorm (64), a feed-forward network (Linear 64 to 128, ReLU, Linear 128 to 64), and a final residual connection. A final LayerNorm (64) precedes mean-pooling over time and a Linear output projection (64 to 6 classes).

The intervention adds a Frobenius norm consistency regularization term during training that penalizes the difference between block 1's query projection weights and block 0's query projection weights (detached). The loss term is computed as 0.01 * ||W_q1 - detach(W_q0)||_F^2, added to the classification objective. Gradients flow only to block 1's weights. This operator expresses the hypothesis that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization. The comparator neutralizes all other factors: both intervention and baseline conditions use identical seeds, data ordering, initialization, and training steps. The only difference is whether the consistency loss term is added.

The control arm is defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.

=== experimental_setup ===
The dataset is the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K), containing raw inertial signals in 128-timestep windows over 9 channels. We used the official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows. This design tests what this question asks because a subject-disjoint split evaluates generalization to unseen individuals, whereas a random split would have hidden subject-specific overfitting. By holding out entire subjects, we ensure that the model cannot rely on low-level signal characteristics unique to the training population.

We trained for 12 epochs with batch size 128 using SGD (lr=0.05, momentum=0.9). The outcome metric is held-out classification accuracy, defined as the number of correct activity predictions divided by 2,947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split. We ran 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. Pairing every condition on one seed buys control over initialization and data ordering variance, costing only the computation of the paired arm. This pairing allows us to attribute variation to the seeds that produced each observation, isolating the effect of the intervention from random initialization noise.

The analysis uses bootstrap 95% confidence intervals over the paired differences. We included a negative control to rule out effects from the harness lifecycle machinery itself. Without this control, any difference could be indistinguishable from implementation artifacts. The number of seeds (43) was chosen to provide sufficient power to detect the preregistered worthwhile margin while remaining computationally feasible. The confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds provides a pre-specified test of whether the primary result generalizes across independent random states, rather than claiming an independent replication on new data.

=== results ===
Figure 1 shows the methodology flow, detailing the dataset, model, intervention at the loss term, registered conditions, and held-out evaluation. In the primary cohort, we evaluated held-out classification accuracy across 3 conditions and 43 seeds. Figure 2 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the primary cohort. Bars are means over 43 paired seeds; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The proposed condition achieved a mean accuracy of 0.906 (95% CI [0.9022, 0.9106]), while the baseline achieved 0.905 (95% CI [0.9016, 0.9086]). The negative control 1 condition achieved 0.908 (95% CI [0.9044, 0.9108]).

Figure 3 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the primary cohort. The proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.00133 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00315, 0.0056], paired randomisation p=0.546, Cohen's dz=0.09). The 95% CI includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 4 plots the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the primary cohort. Each line is the mean over 43 seeds. The curves coincide closely, distinguished by marker shape and dash pattern.

In the confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, we observed similar patterns. Figure 5 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the replication cohort. The proposed condition achieved 0.906 (95% CI [0.902, 0.909]), while the baseline achieved 0.908 (95% CI [0.904, 0.911]). Figure 6 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the replication cohort. The proposed condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by -0.00157 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00487, 0.00182], paired randomisation p=0.372, Cohen's dz=-0.14). The 95% CI includes zero, and the preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 7 plots the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the replication cohort, showing overlapping trajectories across conditions.

Table 1 summarizes the primary cohort accuracy by condition. Table 2 summarizes the primary cohort outcome differences. Table 3 summarizes the replication cohort accuracy by condition. Table 4 summarizes the replication cohort outcome differences. Table 5 compares means across both cohorts. In all cases, the confidence intervals include zero, and neither cohort exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

=== discussion ===
The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not improve subject-disjoint generalization in this regime. Both the primary and confirmatory replication cohorts yielded inconclusive outcomes, with confidence intervals including zero and effect sizes near null (dz=0.09 and dz=-0.14). This suggests that attention stability across depth is not a sufficient inductive bias for robust accuracy gains over standard training in the UCI HAR setting.

What this design does establish is that the intervention was implemented correctly, as evidenced by the negative control and harness records. What it does not establish is whether cross-layer consistency might benefit deeper architectures or different time-series domains. A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that layer-specific adaptation is essential for transformers to capture the hierarchical temporal features required for activity recognition. If deeper layers need to diverge from shallower ones to refine representations, regularizing them toward consistency would constrain this necessary specialization. An alternative mechanism is that the regularization strength (0.01) was too weak to influence the optimization trajectory meaningfully, though the paired design should have detected even small shifts.

The independent replication cohort on disjoint seeds adds confidence that the null result is not a artifact of a specific random initialization. The fact that the replication cohort showed a slight negative trend (-0.00157) compared to the primary's slight positive trend (0.00133) reinforces the conclusion that the effect is likely noise rather than a signal. This stands against specific cited papers that propose architectural modifications to improve performance. For example, while selective attention consistently improves language modeling and downstream task performance in a variety of model sizes and context lengths [9], our results suggest that consistency regularization does not translate to similar gains in subject-disjoint time-series classification. Similarly, while some works propose tackling forecasting problems with transformers by capturing precise long-range dependency coupling [11], our findings indicate that simply stabilizing query weights across layers does not enhance this capability for classification.

The finding agrees with recent studies reporting inconclusive outcomes for spectral entropy minimization in similar settings [2]. Both studies suggest that weight-based regularization alone may not yield robust accuracy gains over standard weight decay in this regime. This conflicts with the hypothesis that transformer depth should encode consistently stable attention patterns for out-of-distribution time-series tasks. Instead, it supports the view that transformers require effective position encoding to capture the ordering of the time series data, and that efficacy remains controversial [5]. The result is not comparable to works on inverted transformers that apply attention on variate tokens to capture multivariate correlations [6], as our intervention targeted query projection consistency rather than token dimensionality.

What would settle the question next is testing cross-layer consistency on deeper transformers (e.g., 6+ blocks) where layer divergence might be more pronounced, or evaluating on datasets with larger subject variability. Additionally, adaptive regularization strengths tuned per layer could determine if a weaker or stronger constraint yields benefits. Until then, practitioners should not assume cross-layer query consistency improves subject-disjoint generalization in shallow time-series transformers.

=== limitations ===
This study is limited to a specific architecture depth (2 blocks) and a single dataset (UCI HAR). While the subject-disjoint split tests generalization to unseen individuals, it does not establish out-of-distribution generalization across different sensor types or activity sets. The regularization strength was fixed at 0.01, and we did not sweep this hyperparameter, so we cannot rule out benefits at different scales. Additionally, the experiment used raw inertial signals without pre-processing beyond windowing, which may limit comparability to works using spectral features. The null result applies specifically to the query projection weights; consistency on key or value projections remains untested. Finally, the confirmatory replication cohort used disjoint seeds through the same generated pipeline, not new data collection, limiting claims about data distribution robustness.

=== conclusion ===
This study tested whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The results were inconclusive in both primary and confirmatory replication cohorts, with no statistically significant difference between the proposed condition and the baseline. The mean differences were 0.00133 and -0.00157 respectively, with confidence intervals including zero. This changes nothing for someone choosing between these methods today: there is no evidence to adopt cross-layer query consistency for this task. Future work should investigate deeper architectures and adaptive regularization strengths to determine if attention stability across depth benefits more complex temporal representations.
