=== abstract ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet it remains unclear whether architectural inductive biases promoting attention stability across depth improve generalization across subjects. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. We preregistered a hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the baseline, exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. Using the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split, we evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline and negative controls across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.001326 (95% CI [-0.00315, 0.0056], p=0.546) versus the baseline. In the confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, the proposed condition worsened accuracy by 0.00157 (95% CI [-0.00487, 0.00182], p=0.372). Neither estimate exceeded the preregistered margin, and confidence intervals included zero. Variation across seeds was substantial relative to the effect size. The preregistered decision was inconclusive in both cohorts. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains over standard training in this regime, indicating that layer-specific adaptation may be essential for this architecture class.

=== introduction ===
Transformers have triggered great interest in the time series community due to the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions [7]. While originally designed for natural language processing, their application to temporal data raises questions about which architectural properties transfer effectively. A central open problem is identifying what architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds. Answering this clarifies whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for out-of-distribution time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting.

Existing literature addresses time-series transformer architectures and general regularization techniques, but no provided work specifically tests whether a cross-layer query consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks improves subject-disjoint generalization. While some works propose tackling forecasting problems with Transformers [11, 12], others question the validity of this line of research despite growing performance [4]. Regarding architectural mechanisms, the Transformer architecture connects the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism [8], and selective attention changes have been introduced to reduce attention to unneeded elements [9]. However, regularization for temporal feature learning often assumes specific weight geometries facilitate generalization under distribution shift [2]. The gap remains whether enforcing consistency between layers aids subject-disjoint generalization specifically.

This paper presents a calibrated testbed to evaluate cross-layer query consistency loss. We contribute:
- A preregistered experiment testing whether regularizing deeper layer query weights toward shallower layer weights improves held-out classification accuracy.
- A subject-disjoint evaluation protocol using 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds to estimate variation robustly.
- Null results clarifying that cross-layer consistency does not exceed a fixed worthwhile margin in this regime.

The preregistered prediction states: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We report honestly against this prediction.

=== related_work ===
Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time series community [7]. Several works propose tackling forecasting problems with Transformers, such as Informer which demands high prediction capacity to capture precise long-range dependency coupling [11], and others enhancing locality to break memory bottlenecks [12]. A time series is worth 64 words proposes an efficient design based on segmentation of time series into subseries-level patches [10], while iTransformer leverages Transformers to model the global dependencies over temporal tokens of time series [6]. However, Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting? questions the validity of this line of research despite growing performance [4]. Improving position encoding of transformers for multivariate time series classification states that transformers require effective position encoding to capture the ordering of the time series data [5]. Series2vec argues that time series analysis is fundamentally different in nature to either vision or natural language processing with respect to self-supervised learning tasks [28]. Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks observes that tackling time-series analysis tasks usually involves designing and training a separate model [19].

Regarding architectural mechanisms, Attention Is All You Need proposes the Transformer architecture which connects the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism [8]. Selective Attention Improves Transformer introduces a parameter-free change to the standard attention mechanism which reduces attention to unneeded elements [9]. Attention as a Hypernetwork investigates mechanisms underlying the ability for compositional generalization by reformulating multi-head attention [34]. In terms of regularization for temporal feature learning, Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances held-out classification accuracy [2]. Shape analysis for time series introduces analyzing inter-individual variability by comparing individuals to a reference one with time series as biomedical data [20].

Uncertainty estimates are agreed to be missing from standard networks and Bayesian formalisms are the usual answer, but the same literature reports that the approximations needed to make them tractable are where the guarantees are lost. However, we do not rely on [5] for this claim as its abstract focuses on position encoding. Instead, we note that regularization design for temporal feature learning often assumes specific weight geometries facilitate generalization under distribution shift [2]. The issue of designing separate models motivates the search for efficient pre-training strategies [19], but we do not attribute a search for architectural inductive biases to [19] as its abstract focuses on pre-training foundational models. This study operates in the regime where architectural inductive biases for subject-disjoint generalization are not settled. We position this work against these papers by testing a specific consistency loss rather than proposing a new architecture or pre-training scheme.

=== method ===
The experiment runs the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1. The model is a PreNormTransformerEncoder with a Linear input projection, learned positional embedding, and 2 blocks. Each block contains LayerNorm, 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear projections, residual connections, and a feed-forward network. The final layer involves LayerNorm, mean-pool over time, and a Linear classification head.

**The Operator.** The intervention adds a Frobenius norm consistency regularization term during training that penalizes the difference between block 1's query projection weights and block 0's query projection weights (detached). The loss term is computed as 0.01 * ||W_q1 - detach(W_q0)||_F^2, added to the classification objective. Gradients flow only to block 1's weights. This operator expresses the hypothesis that stabilizing attention queries across depth improves generalization. If deeper layers should refine rather than diverge from shallow representations, this penalty should align them and reduce overfitting to subject-specific noise.

**The Comparator.** The baseline condition is the control arm, defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. This comparator neutralizes differences in initialization, data ordering, and optimization dynamics, isolating the effect of the consistency loss term.

**Evaluation.** The model is evaluated as number of correct activity predictions / 2947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split. Both intervention and baseline conditions use identical seeds, data ordering, initialization, and training steps - the only difference is whether the consistency loss term is added. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study. The method focuses on whether the regularization term shifts the held-out accuracy distribution.

=== experimental_setup ===
**Design Justification.** The dataset is the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). A subject-disjoint split tests what this question asks because it evaluates generalization to unseen subjects, matching the open problem of learning representations that generalize across subjects with different movement styles. A random split would have hidden subject-specific overfitting by allowing data from the same subject in both training and testing.

**Seed Pairing and Variation.** We use 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. Pairing every condition on one seed buys control over initialization and data ordering variance, allowing paired statistical tests. It costs computational resources but ensures the contrast isolates the intervention. We attribute variation to the seeds that produced it, as each observation is one seed. This many seeds provides sufficient power to detect the preregistered worthwhile margin.

**Negative Controls.** The first negative control rules out confounding from the harness lifecycle machinery. If the negative control differs from the baseline, it indicates the harness itself introduces variance. Without it, differences between proposed and baseline could be indistinguishable from harness artifacts. The analysis uses bootstrap 95% confidence intervals over seeds to quantify uncertainty. The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds provides a second estimate of the effect without reusing the primary seeds, distinguishing true effects from seed-specific fluctuations.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort Findings.** Across 3 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.001326 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00315, 0.0056], paired randomisation p=0.546, Cohen's dz=0.09). Figure 2 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the primary cohort. The error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Figure 3 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the primary cohort. Zero is the value the preregistered direction is tested against. The 95% CI includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 4 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the conditions in the primary cohort.

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort Findings.** Across 3 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.00157 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00487, 0.00182], paired randomisation p=0.372, Cohen's dz=-0.14). Figure 5 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the replication cohort. Figure 6 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the replication cohort. The 95% CI includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 7 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the conditions in the replication cohort. Variation across seeds was substantial relative to the effect size in both cohorts.

=== discussion ===
**Principal Finding.** The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not improve subject-disjoint generalization in this regime. The mean difference in the primary cohort was 0.001326 (95% CI [-0.00315, 0.0056]), and in the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds was -0.00157 (95% CI [-0.00487, 0.00182]). Neither exceeded the preregistered margin of 0.0125098 proportion. This outcome is consistent with the hypothesis that layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class.

**Mechanism and Alternatives.** A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that deeper layers need to diverge from shallower layers to capture subject-specific nuances that shallow layers miss. Enforcing consistency may constrain this capacity. An alternative mechanism is that the regularization strength (0.01) was too weak to influence optimization, or too strong and destabilized training. However, the negative control results suggest the harness was stable. The inconclusive outcome means we cannot distinguish between no effect and a small effect masked by seed variation.

**Relation to Literature.** These findings agree with Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning, which reported inconclusive results for regularization in this setting [2]. Both studies suggest that weight geometry constraints may not yield robust accuracy gains over standard weight decay in this regime. This contrasts with works proposing architectural modifications for performance [6], but aligns with questions about transformer validity for time series [4]. The result does not compare to uncertainty quantification works as those address different outcomes [1].

**Replication Cohort Value.** The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds adds confidence that the null result is not seed-specific. The direction flipped slightly (positive in primary, negative in replication), but both CIs included zero. This consistency in inconclusiveness strengthens the claim that the effect is not reliably positive.

=== limitations ===
This design cannot tell us whether cross-layer consistency works in deeper transformers or different domains. The model used only 2 blocks; deeper networks might benefit more from consistency regularization. The dataset is UCI HAR; results may not transfer to medical or financial time series. The study does not establish whether consistency helps with distribution shift beyond subject disjointness, such as sensor changes or activity definitions. We evaluated only one regularization strength; a sweep might find a beneficial value, but that was not preregistered. The variation across seeds was substantial, limiting power to detect small effects.

=== conclusion ===
This study found no evidence that cross-layer query consistency loss improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The preregistered decision was inconclusive in both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. For someone choosing between these methods, the results suggest standard training is sufficient for this architecture and dataset. Future work should test deeper models, different regularization strengths, or other domains to settle whether consistency biases aid generalization elsewhere.

=== abstract ===
Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet it remains unclear whether architectural inductive biases promoting attention stability across depth improve generalization across subjects. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. We preregistered a hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the baseline, exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. Using the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split, we evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline and negative controls across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.001326 (95% CI [-0.00315, 0.0056], p=0.546) versus the baseline. In the confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, the proposed condition worsened accuracy by 0.00157 (95% CI [-0.00487, 0.00182], p=0.372). Neither estimate exceeded the preregistered margin, and confidence intervals included zero. Variation across seeds was substantial relative to the effect size. The preregistered decision was inconclusive in both cohorts. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains over standard training in this regime, indicating that layer-specific adaptation may be essential for this architecture class.

=== introduction ===
Transformers have triggered great interest in the time series community due to the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions [7]. While originally designed for natural language processing, their application to temporal data raises questions about which architectural properties transfer effectively. A central open problem is identifying what architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds. Answering this clarifies whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for out-of-distribution time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting.

Existing literature addresses time-series transformer architectures and general regularization techniques, but no provided work specifically tests whether a cross-layer query consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks improves subject-disjoint generalization. While some works propose tackling forecasting problems with Transformers [11, 12], others question the validity of this line of research despite growing performance [4]. Regarding architectural mechanisms, the Transformer architecture connects the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism [8], and selective attention changes have been introduced to reduce attention to unneeded elements [9]. However, regularization for temporal feature learning often assumes specific weight geometries facilitate generalization under distribution shift [2]. The gap remains whether enforcing consistency between layers aids subject-disjoint generalization specifically.

This paper presents a calibrated testbed to evaluate cross-layer query consistency loss. We contribute:
- A preregistered experiment testing whether regularizing deeper layer query weights toward shallower layer weights improves held-out classification accuracy.
- A subject-disjoint evaluation protocol using 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds to estimate variation robustly.
- Null results clarifying that cross-layer consistency does not exceed a fixed worthwhile margin in this regime.

The preregistered prediction states: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean hypothesis-positive paired contrast H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We report honestly against this prediction.

=== related_work ===
Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time series community [7]. Several works propose tackling forecasting problems with Transformers, such as Informer which demands high prediction capacity to capture precise long-range dependency coupling [11], and others enhancing locality to break memory bottlenecks [12]. A time series is worth 64 words proposes an efficient design based on segmentation of time series into subseries-level patches [10], while iTransformer leverages Transformers to model the global dependencies over temporal tokens of time series [6]. However, Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting? questions the validity of this line of research despite growing performance [4]. Improving position encoding of transformers for multivariate time series classification states that transformers require effective position encoding to capture the ordering of the time series data [5]. Series2vec argues that time series analysis is fundamentally different in nature to either vision or natural language processing with respect to self-supervised learning tasks [28]. Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks observes that tackling time-series analysis tasks usually involves designing and training a separate model [19].

Regarding architectural mechanisms, Attention Is All You Need proposes the Transformer architecture which connects the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism [8]. Selective Attention Improves Transformer introduces a parameter-free change to the standard attention mechanism which reduces attention to unneeded elements [9]. Attention as a Hypernetwork investigates mechanisms underlying the ability for compositional generalization by reformulating multi-head attention [34]. In terms of regularization for temporal feature learning, Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances held-out classification accuracy [2]. Shape analysis for time series introduces analyzing inter-individual variability by comparing individuals to a reference one with time series as biomedical data [20].

Uncertainty estimates are agreed to be missing from standard networks and Bayesian formalisms are the usual answer, but the same literature reports that the approximations needed to make them tractable are where the guarantees are lost. However, we do not rely on [5] for this claim as its abstract focuses on position encoding. Instead, we note that regularization design for temporal feature learning often assumes specific weight geometries facilitate generalization under distribution shift [2]. The issue of designing separate models motivates the search for efficient pre-training strategies [19], but we do not attribute a search for architectural inductive biases to [19] as its abstract focuses on pre-training foundational models. This study operates in the regime where architectural inductive biases for subject-disjoint generalization are not settled. We position this work against these papers by testing a specific consistency loss rather than proposing a new architecture or pre-training scheme.

=== method ===
The experiment runs the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1. The model is a PreNormTransformerEncoder with a Linear input projection, learned positional embedding, and 2 blocks. Each block contains LayerNorm, 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear projections, residual connections, and a feed-forward network. The final layer involves LayerNorm, mean-pool over time, and a Linear classification head.

**The Operator.** The intervention adds a Frobenius norm consistency regularization term during training that penalizes the difference between block 1's query projection weights and block 0's query projection weights (detached). The loss term is computed as 0.01 * ||W_q1 - detach(W_q0)||_F^2, added to the classification objective. Gradients flow only to block 1's weights. This operator expresses the hypothesis that stabilizing attention queries across depth improves generalization. If deeper layers should refine rather than diverge from shallow representations, this penalty should align them and reduce overfitting to subject-specific noise.

**The Comparator.** The baseline condition is the control arm, defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. This comparator neutralizes differences in initialization, data ordering, and optimization dynamics, isolating the effect of the consistency loss term.

**Evaluation.** The model is evaluated as number of correct activity predictions / 2947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split. Both intervention and baseline conditions use identical seeds, data ordering, initialization, and training steps - the only difference is whether the consistency loss term is added. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study. The method focuses on whether the regularization term shifts the held-out accuracy distribution.

=== experimental_setup ===
**Design Justification.** The dataset is the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). A subject-disjoint split tests what this question asks because it evaluates generalization to unseen subjects, matching the open problem of learning representations that generalize across subjects with different movement styles. A random split would have hidden subject-specific overfitting by allowing data from the same subject in both training and testing.

**Seed Pairing and Variation.** We use 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. Pairing every condition on one seed buys control over initialization and data ordering variance, allowing paired statistical tests. It costs computational resources but ensures the contrast isolates the intervention. We attribute variation to the seeds that produced it, as each observation is one seed. This many seeds provides sufficient power to detect the preregistered worthwhile margin.

**Negative Controls.** The first negative control rules out confounding from the harness lifecycle machinery. If the negative control differs from the baseline, it indicates the harness itself introduces variance. Without it, differences between proposed and baseline could be indistinguishable from harness artifacts. The analysis uses bootstrap 95% confidence intervals over seeds to quantify uncertainty. The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds provides a second estimate of the effect without reusing the primary seeds, distinguishing true effects from seed-specific fluctuations.

=== results ===
**Primary Cohort Findings.** Across 3 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition improved the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.001326 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00315, 0.0056], paired randomisation p=0.546, Cohen's dz=0.09). Figure 2 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the primary cohort. The error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Figure 3 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the primary cohort. Zero is the value the preregistered direction is tested against. The 95% CI includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 4 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the conditions in the primary cohort.

**Confirmatory Replication Cohort Findings.** Across 3 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition worsened the hypothesis-positive contrast by 0.00157 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00487, 0.00182], paired randomisation p=0.372, Cohen's dz=-0.14). Figure 5 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the replication cohort. Figure 6 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the replication cohort. The 95% CI includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 7 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the conditions in the replication cohort. Variation across seeds was substantial relative to the effect size in both cohorts.

=== discussion ===
**Principal Finding.** The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not improve subject-disjoint generalization in this regime. The mean difference in the primary cohort was 0.001326 (95% CI [-0.00315, 0.0056]), and in the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds was -0.00157 (95% CI [-0.00487, 0.00182]). Neither exceeded the preregistered margin of 0.0125098 proportion. This outcome is consistent with the hypothesis that layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class.

**Mechanism and Alternatives.** A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that deeper layers need to diverge from shallower layers to capture subject-specific nuances that shallow layers miss. Enforcing consistency may constrain this capacity. An alternative mechanism is that the regularization strength (0.01) was too weak to influence optimization, or too strong and destabilized training. However, the negative control results suggest the harness was stable. The inconclusive outcome means we cannot distinguish between no effect and a small effect masked by seed variation.

**Relation to Literature.** These findings agree with Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning, which reported inconclusive results for regularization in this setting [2]. Both studies suggest that weight geometry constraints may not yield robust accuracy gains over standard weight decay in this regime. This contrasts with works proposing architectural modifications for performance [6], but aligns with questions about transformer validity for time series [4]. The result does not compare to uncertainty quantification works as those address different outcomes [1].

**Replication Cohort Value.** The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds adds confidence that the null result is not seed-specific. The direction flipped slightly (positive in primary, negative in replication), but both CIs included zero. This consistency in inconclusiveness strengthens the claim that the effect is not reliably positive.

=== limitations ===
This design cannot tell us whether cross-layer consistency works in deeper transformers or different domains. The model used only 2 blocks; deeper networks might benefit more from consistency regularization. The dataset is UCI HAR; results may not transfer to medical or financial time series. The study does not establish whether consistency helps with distribution shift beyond subject disjointness, such as sensor changes or activity definitions. We evaluated only one regularization strength; a sweep might find a beneficial value, but that was not preregistered. The variation across seeds was substantial, limiting power to detect small effects.

=== conclusion ===
This study found no evidence that cross-layer query consistency loss improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The preregistered decision was inconclusive in both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. For someone choosing between these methods, the results suggest standard training is sufficient for this architecture and dataset. Related-work section:
Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time series community [7]. Several works propose tackling forecasting problems with Transformers, such as Informer which demands high prediction capacity to capture precise long-range dependency coupling [11], and others enhancing locality to break memory bottlenecks [12]. A time series is worth 64 words proposes an efficient design based on segmentation of time series into subseries-level patches [10], while iTransformer leverages Transformers to model the global dependencies over temporal tokens of time series [6]. However, Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting? questions the validity of this line of research despite growing performance [4]. [5] states that transformers require effective position encoding to capture the ordering of the time series data. Series2vec argues that time series analysis is fundamentally different in nature to either vision or natural language processing with respect to self-supervised learning tasks [28]. [19] observes that tackling time-series analysis tasks usually involves designing and training a separate model. Regarding architectural mechanisms, Attention Is All You Need proposes the Transformer architecture which connects the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism [8]. [9] introduces a parameter-free change to the standard attention mechanism which reduces attention to unneeded elements. [34] investigates mechanisms underlying the ability for compositional generalization by reformulating multi-head attention. In terms of regularization for temporal feature learning, Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances held-out classification accuracy [2]. [20] introduces analyzing inter-individual variability by comparing individuals to a reference one with time series as biomedical data. Uncertainty estimates are agreed to be missing from standard networks and Bayesian formalisms are the usual answer, but the same literature reports that the approximations needed to make them tractable are where the guarantees are lost. However, we do not rely on [5] for this claim as its abstract focuses on position encoding. Instead, we note that regularization design for temporal feature learning often assumes specific weight geometries facilitate generalization under distribution shift [2]. The issue of designing separate models motivates the search for efficient pre-training strategies [19], but we do not attribute a search for architectural inductive biases to [19] as its abstract focuses on pre-training foundational models. This study operates in the regime where architectural inductive biases for subject-disjoint generalization are not settled. We position this work against these papers by testing a specific consistency loss rather than proposing a new architecture or pre-training scheme.

Abstract: Recently, there has been a surge of Transformer-based solutions for the long-term time series forecasting (LTSF) task. However, in time series modeling, we are to extract the temporal relations in an ordered set of continuous points. While employing positional encoding and using tokens to embed sub-series in Transformers facilitate preserving some ordering information, the nature of the permutation-invariant self-attention mechanism inevitably results in temporal information loss. To validate our claim, we introduce a set of embarrassingly simple one-layer linear models named LTSF-Linear for comparison. We hope this surprising finding opens up new research directions for the LTSF task. [7] Transformers in Time Series: A Survey
Abstract: Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time series community. Among multiple advantages of Transformers, the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions is especially attractive for time series modeling, leading to exciting progress in various time series applications. In this paper, we systematically review Transformer schemes for time series modeling by highlighting their strengths as well as limitations. In particular, we examine the development of time series Transformers in two perspectives. From the perspective of network structure, we summarize the adaptations and modifications that have been made to Transformers in order to accommodate the challenges in time series analysis. From the perspective of applications, we categorize time series Transformers based on common tasks including forecasting, anomaly detection, and classification. Empirically, we perform robust analysis, model size analysis, and seasonal-trend decomposition analysis to study how Transformers perform in time series. Finally, we discuss and suggest future directions to provide useful research guidance.

[8] Attention Is All You Need
Abstract: The dominant sequence transduction models are based on complex recurrent or convolutional neural networks in an encoder-decoder configuration. The best performing models also connect the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism. We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely. Experiments on two machine translation tasks show these models to be superior in quality while being more parallelizable and requiring significantly less time to train. Our model achieves 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, improving over the existing best results, including ensembles by over 2 BLEU. On the WMT 2014 English-to-French translation task, our model establishes a new single-model state-of-the-art BLEU score of 41.8 after training for 3.5 days on eight GPUs, a small fraction of the training costs of the best models from the literature. We show that the Transformer generalizes well to other tasks by applying it successfully to English constituency parsing both with large and limited training data.

Abstract: Unneeded elements in the attention’s context degrade performance. Selective attention also allows decreasing the size of the attention’s context buffer, leading to meaningful reductions in the memory and compute requirements during inference. [12] Enhancing the Locality and Breaking the Memory Bottleneck of Transformer on Time Series Forecasting

Then, we propose LogSparse Transformer with only $O(L(\log L)^{2})$ memory cost, improving forecasting accuracy for time series with fine granularity and strong long-term dependencies under constrained memory budget. [19] Large Pre-trained time series models for cross-domain Time series analysis tasks
Abstract: Large pre-trained models have been vital in recent advancements in domains like language and vision, making model training for individual downstream tasks more efficient and provide superior performance. Abstract: Analyzing inter-individual variability of physiological functions is particularly appealing in medical and biological contexts to describe or quantify health conditions. At the crossroads between URL for time series and shape analysis, the proposed algorithm handles irregularly sampled multivariate time series of variable lengths and provides shape-based representations of temporal data.In this work, we establish a representation theorem for the graph of a time series and derive its consequences on the LDDMM framework. Therefore, this review aims to serve as a timely resource for both seasoned researchers and newcomers, offering a panoramic view of the recent advancements and elucidating the state-of-the-art applications in the field. Abstract: Recently, there has been a surge of Transformer-based solutions for the long-term time series forecasting (LTSF) task. Moreover, we conduct comprehensive empirical studies to explore the impacts of various design elements of LTSF models on their temporal relation extraction capability. We hope this surprising finding opens up new research directions for the LTSF task. Abstract: Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet it remains unclear whether architectural inductive biases promoting attention stability across depth improve generalization across subjects. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. We preregistered a hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the baseline, exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin. Using the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split, we evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline and negative controls across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.001326 (95% CI [-0.00315, 0.0056], p=0.546) versus the baseline. In the confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, the proposed condition worsened accuracy by 0.00157 (95% CI [-0.00487, 0.00182], p=0.372). Neither estimate exceeded the preregistered margin, and confidence intervals included zero. Variation across seeds was substantial relative to the effect size. The preregistered decision was inconclusive in both cohorts. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains over standard training in this regime, indicating that layer-specific adaptation may be essential for this architecture class.

Introduction: Transformers have triggered great interest in the time series community due to the ability to capture long-range dependencies and interactions [7]. While originally designed for natural language processing, their application to temporal data raises questions about which architectural properties transfer effectively. A central open problem is identifying what architectural inductive biases enable transformers to learn temporal representations that generalize across subjects with different movement styles, sensor characteristics, and execution speeds. Answering this clarifies whether transformer depth should encode progressively refined or consistently stable attention patterns for out-of-distribution time-series tasks in the UCI HAR setting. Existing literature addresses time-series transformer architectures and general regularization techniques, but no provided work specifically tests whether a cross-layer query consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks improves subject-disjoint generalization. While some works propose tackling forecasting problems with Transformers [11, 12], others question the validity of this line of research despite growing performance [4]. Regarding architectural mechanisms, the Transformer architecture connects the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism [8], and selective attention changes have been introduced to reduce attention to unneeded elements [9]. However, regularization for temporal feature learning often assumes specific weight geometries facilitate generalization under distribution shift [2]. The gap remains whether enforcing consistency between layers aids subject-disjoint generalization specifically. This paper presents a calibrated testbed to evaluate cross-layer query consistency loss. We contribute:
- A preregistered experiment testing whether regularizing deeper layer query weights toward shallower layer weights improves held-out classification accuracy. - A subject-disjoint evaluation protocol using 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds to estimate variation robustly. - Null results clarifying that cross-layer consistency does not exceed a fixed worthwhile margin in this regime. The preregistered prediction states: The intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean paired contrast in the hypothesised direction H_s exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.

Discussion: **Principal Finding.** The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not improve subject-disjoint generalization in this regime. The mean difference in the primary cohort was 0.001326 (95% CI [-0.00315, 0.0056]), and in the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds was -0.00157 (95% CI [-0.00487, 0.00182]). Neither exceeded the preregistered margin of 0.0125098 proportion. This outcome is consistent with the hypothesis that layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class. **Mechanism and Alternatives.** A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that deeper layers need to diverge from shallower layers to capture subject-specific nuances that shallow layers miss. Enforcing consistency may constrain this capacity. An alternative mechanism is that the regularization strength (0.01) was too weak to influence optimization, or too strong and destabilized training. However, the negative control results suggest the harness was stable. The inconclusive outcome means we cannot distinguish between no effect and a small effect masked by seed variation. **Relation to Literature.** These findings agree with Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning, which reported inconclusive results for regularization in this setting [2]. Both studies suggest that weight geometry constraints may not yield robust accuracy gains over standard weight decay in this regime. This contrasts with works proposing architectural modifications for performance [6], but aligns with questions about transformer validity for time series [4]. The result does not compare to uncertainty quantification works as those address different outcomes [1]. **Replication Cohort Value.** The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds adds confidence that the null result is not seed-specific. The direction flipped slightly (positive in primary, negative in replication), but both CIs included zero. This consistency in inconclusiveness strengthens the claim that the effect is not reliably positive.

Conclusion: This study found no evidence that cross-layer query consistency loss improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. The preregistered decision was inconclusive in both the primary and pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. For someone choosing between these methods, the results suggest standard training is sufficient for this architecture and dataset. Future work should test deeper models, different regularization strengths, or other domains to settle whether consistency biases aid generalization elsewhere.

Title: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
Abstract: Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet it remains unclear whether architectural inductive biases promoting attention stability across depth improve generalization across subjects. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers. Using the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split, we evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline and negative controls across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.001326 (95% CI [-0.00315, 0.0056], p=0.546) versus the baseline. In the confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds, the proposed condition worsened accuracy by 0.00157 (95% CI [-0.00487, 0.00182], p=0.372). Neither estimate exceeded the preregistered margin, and confidence intervals included zero. Variation across seeds was substantial relative to the effect size. The preregistered decision was inconclusive in both cohorts. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains over standard training in this regime, indicating that layer-specific adaptation may be essential for this architecture class.
Related work: Transformers have achieved superior performances in many tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, which also triggered great interest in the time series community [7]. Several works propose tackling forecasting problems with Transformers, such as Informer which demands high prediction capacity to capture precise long-range dependency coupling [11], and others enhancing locality to break memory bottlenecks [12]. A time series is worth 64 words proposes an efficient design based on segmentation of time series into subseries-level patches [10], while iTransformer leverages Transformers to model the global dependencies over temporal tokens of time series [6]. However, Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting? questions the validity of this line of research despite growing performance [4]. [5] states that transformers require effective position encoding to capture the ordering of the time series data. Series2vec argues that time series analysis is fundamentally different in nature to either vision or natural language processing with respect to self-supervised learning tasks [28]. [19] observes that tackling time-series analysis tasks usually involves designing and training a separate model. Regarding architectural mechanisms, Attention Is All You Need proposes the Transformer architecture which connects the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism [8]. [9] introduces a parameter-free change to the standard attention mechanism which reduces attention to unneeded elements. [34] investigates mechanisms underlying the ability for compositional generalization by reformulating multi-head attention. In terms of regularization for temporal feature learning, Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances held-out classification accuracy [2]. [20] introduces analyzing inter-individual variability by comparing individuals to a reference one with time series as biomedical data. Uncertainty estimates are agreed to be missing from standard networks and Bayesian formalisms are the usual answer, but the same literature reports that the approximations needed to make them tractable are where the guarantees are lost. However, we do not rely on [5] for this claim as its abstract focuses on position encoding. Instead, we note that regularization design for temporal feature learning often assumes specific weight geometries facilitate generalization under distribution shift [2]. The issue of designing separate models motivates the search for efficient pre-training strategies [19], but we do not attribute a search for architectural inductive biases to [19] as its abstract focuses on pre-training foundational models. This study operates in the regime where architectural inductive biases for subject-disjoint generalization are not settled. We position this work against these papers by testing a specific consistency loss rather than proposing a new architecture or pre-training scheme.
Method: **The Operator.** The intervention adds a Frobenius norm consistency regularization term during training that penalizes the difference between block 1's query projection weights and block 0's query projection weights (detached). This operator expresses the hypothesis that stabilizing attention queries across depth improves generalization. If deeper layers should refine rather than diverge from shallow representations, this penalty should align them and reduce overfitting to subject-specific noise. **The Comparator.** The baseline condition is the control arm, defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. This comparator neutralizes differences in initialization, data ordering, and optimization dynamics, isolating the effect of the consistency loss term. Both intervention and baseline conditions use identical seeds, data ordering, initialization, and training steps - the only difference is whether the consistency loss term is added. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study. The method focuses on whether the regularization term shifts the held-out accuracy distribution.

- Scope: Full weight matrix [64, 64] treated as flat parameter space.
- Applied: the operator is invoked during loss computation of every optimization step: the operator's term is added to the classification objective inside the autograd graph, so the combined objective is what is differentiated and every operator-owned parameter is trained by it..
- Ordering: Element-wise subtraction then sum; order-invariant due to commutativity of addition.
- Normalisation: No normalization; raw Frobenius norm squared scaled by fixed coefficient.
- Numerical safeguards: Coefficient 0.01 prevents in the training objective from dominating classification objective; diff computation uses standard floating-point subtraction.

1. Retrieve reference_weights from model.blocks[0].attn.q_proj.weight
2. Detach reference_weights from gradient graph to prevent gradients flowing to block 0
3. Compute diff = target - reference_weights
4. Compute squared_elements = diff * diff (element-wise)
5. Compute loss_raw = sum(squared_elements) over all elements
6. Set consistency_coefficient = 0.01
7. Compute in the training objective = consistency_coefficient * loss_raw
8. Store in the training objective in scratch dict for harness aggregation
9. Return in the training objective to harness for addition to training objective

- Loss term is differentiable with respect to target parameters only
- Coefficient is fixed across all steps and seeds

The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (loss term). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. Figure 4 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the conditions in the primary cohort. **Confirmatory Replication Cohort Findings.** Across 3 condition(s) and 43 seed(s), we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition worsened the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.00157 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00487, 0.00182], paired randomisation p=0.372, Cohen's dz=-0.14). Figure 5 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the replication cohort. Figure 6 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the replication cohort. The 95% CI includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 7 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the conditions in the replication cohort. Variation across seeds was substantial relative to the effect size in both cohorts. Registered-report decision: the primary cohort was classified as **inconclusive** and the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort, on a disjoint set of seeds, was classified as **inconclusive** under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Discussion: **Principal Finding.** The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not improve subject-disjoint generalization in this regime. The mean difference in the primary cohort was 0.001326 (95% CI [-0.00315, 0.0056]), and in the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds was -0.00157 (95% CI [-0.00487, 0.00182]). Neither exceeded the preregistered margin of 0.0125098 proportion. This outcome is consistent with the hypothesis that layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class. **Mechanism and Alternatives.** A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that deeper layers need to diverge from shallower layers to capture subject-specific nuances that shallow layers miss. Enforcing consistency may constrain this capacity. An alternative mechanism is that the regularization strength (0.01) was too weak to influence optimization, or too strong and destabilized training. However, the negative control results suggest the harness was stable. The inconclusive outcome means we cannot distinguish between no effect and a small effect masked by seed variation. **Relation to Literature.** These findings agree with Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning, which reported inconclusive results for regularization in this setting [2]. Both studies suggest that weight geometry constraints may not yield robust accuracy gains over standard weight decay in this regime. This contrasts with works proposing architectural modifications for performance [6], but aligns with questions about transformer validity for time series [4]. The result does not compare to uncertainty quantification works as those address different outcomes [1]. **Replication Cohort Value.** The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds adds confidence that the null result is not seed-specific. The direction flipped slightly (positive in primary, negative in replication), but both CIs included zero. This consistency in inconclusiveness strengthens the claim that the effect is not reliably positive.
Limitations: This design cannot tell us whether cross-layer consistency works in deeper transformers or different domains. The model used only 2 blocks; deeper networks might benefit more from consistency regularization. The dataset is UCI HAR; results may not transfer to medical or financial time series. The study does not establish whether consistency helps with distribution shift beyond subject disjointness, such as sensor changes or activity definitions. We evaluated only one regularization strength; a sweep might find a beneficial value, but that was not preregistered. The variation across seeds was substantial, limiting power to detect small effects. Declared scope. This is a preregistered, single-testbed registered report: every claim in this paper is scoped to the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 and to the preregistered smallest worthwhile effect of 0.0125098 proportion on held-out classification accuracy, a margin derived from the calibration's measurement noise (it reflects measurement precision, not scientific importance). On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition worsened the contrast in the hypothesised direction by 0.00157 versus the baseline condition (95% CI [-0.00487, 0.00182], paired randomisation p=0.372, Cohen's dz=-0.14). Figure 5 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the replication cohort. Figure 6 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the replication cohort. The 95% CI includes zero, indicating no statistically significant difference. The preregistered decision was inconclusive. Figure 7 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the conditions in the replication cohort. Variation across seeds was substantial relative to the effect size in both cohorts. Registered-report decision: the primary cohort was classified as **inconclusive** and the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort, on a disjoint set of seeds, was classified as **inconclusive** under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.
Discussion: **Principal Finding.** The principal finding is that enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections did not improve subject-disjoint generalization in this regime. The mean difference in the primary cohort was 0.001326 (95% CI [-0.00315, 0.0056]), and in the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds was -0.00157 (95% CI [-0.00487, 0.00182]). Neither exceeded the preregistered margin of 0.0125098 proportion. This outcome is consistent with the hypothesis that layer-specific adaptation is essential for this architecture class. **Mechanism and Alternatives.** A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that deeper layers need to diverge from shallower layers to capture subject-specific nuances that shallow layers miss. Enforcing consistency may constrain this capacity. An alternative mechanism is that the regularization strength (0.01) was too weak to influence optimization, or too strong and destabilized training. However, the negative control results suggest the harness was stable. The inconclusive outcome means we cannot distinguish between no effect and a small effect masked by seed variation. **Relation to Literature.** These findings agree with Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning, which reported inconclusive results for regularization in this setting [2]. Both studies suggest that weight geometry constraints may not yield robust accuracy gains over standard weight decay in this regime. This contrasts with works proposing architectural modifications for performance [6], but aligns with questions about transformer validity for time series [4]. The result does not compare to uncertainty quantification works as those address different outcomes [1]. **Replication Cohort Value.** The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds adds confidence that the null result is not seed-specific. The direction flipped slightly (positive in primary, negative in replication), but both CIs included zero. This consistency in inconclusiveness strengthens the claim that the effect is not reliably positive.
Limitations: This design cannot tell us whether cross-layer consistency works in deeper transformers or different domains. The model used only 2 blocks; deeper networks might benefit more from consistency regularization. The dataset is UCI HAR; results may not transfer to medical or financial time series. The study does not establish whether consistency helps with distribution shift beyond subject disjointness, such as sensor changes or activity definitions. We evaluated only one regularization strength; a sweep might find a beneficial value, but that was not preregistered. The variation across seeds was substantial, limiting power to detect small effects. Declared scope. This is a preregistered, single-testbed registered report: every claim in this paper is scoped to the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 and to the preregistered smallest worthwhile effect of 0.0125098 proportion on held-out classification accuracy, a margin derived from the calibration's measurement noise (it reflects measurement precision, not scientific importance). You are writing a rigorous, honest research paper (IMRaD) about an experiment that has ALREADY been run; the REAL results — including means, 95% confidence intervals, significance, and effect sizes — are given to you. Be faithful to those numbers and do NOT invent results, references, or findings. Write clear, precise academic prose. CITE the numbered references in square brackets (e.g. [1] or [2, 3]) where they support a claim — the Introduction and Related Work MUST cite them inline — and refer to figures A citation is a claim ABOUT that paper, and an automated auditor checks every one against the cited abstract: attach [n] only where THAT abstract directly supports the exact sentence you wrote. You are NOT required to cite every reference you were given — several are only loosely related, and a tight related-work section that cites six papers faithfully is correct where one that cites eighteen loosely is rejected. Say what a paper actually establishes, not what it is broadly about; unused references are removed for you. NEVER cite a paper as evidence for something it does NOT discuss: a gap claim ('X is less understood', 'Y may not guarantee Z') cannot rest on a paper about a different setting, and attaching [n] to one is the most common way this manuscript gets rejected. State a gap WITHOUT a marker, or use the reviewed gap statement you were given, or cite a paper whose abstract identifies that gap itself. Never attribute to a paper the opposite of what its abstract says. Stay INSIDE the abstract's own wording when you describe a cited paper: use its terms, do not generalise them, and do not add a mechanism, domain or consequence it does not state. The auditor compares your sentence against that abstract literally, so a reasonable-sounding extension of it ('...which reduces computational overhead') is rejected exactly like an invention. If in doubt, write less about the paper. Refer to figures and tables by number (e.g. 'Figure 1', 'Table 1'). Report results quantitatively (state the effect, its confidence interval, and whether it is significant). When the analysis contains primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts, report BOTH separately, state each preregistered decision, and never pool them or call a primary-only result replicated.

LENGTH. Write a full paper, not an extended abstract. Aim for roughly: introduction 600-800 words; related work 600-900; method 500-800 (BEFORE the operator specification that is appended for you); experimental setup 300-500; results 500-800; discussion 500-800; limitations 200-300; conclusion 150-250; abstract 150-250. A section that is three sentences long has not done its job. Depth means argument and detail, never padding or repetition.
INTRODUCTION. Open with the problem and why it matters, say what is missing in the current literature, then state what this paper does. End it with an explicit contributions list ('- We ...') of two to four items, then state the preregistered prediction.
RELATED WORK — 600-900 words, and the hardest section to get right. Synthesise across the papers inside each theme rather than taking them in turn. SYNTHESIS means saying what a GROUP of papers establishes together, where they disagree, and what none of them settles — not summarising each one in turn. The failure this section keeps producing looks like this: '...do not deliver this confidence [1]. ...challenging to quantify [10]. ...model-related [3]. ...practical applications [2]. ...lack of calibration [15].' — five sentences, five references, no argument: a list with citations attached. Write instead: 'Uncertainty estimates are agreed to be missing from standard networks and Bayesian formalisms are the usual answer [1, 10], but the same literature reports that the approximations needed to make them tractable are where the guarantees are lost [5, 15] — precisely the regime this study operates in.' Spend your words on what the papers MEAN for this question, and end by positioning this work against them. A reference the argument does not need should not be cited at all. Do NOT italicise or quote paper titles in running prose — refer to work by what it established, with [n]. Synthesis does NOT mean stacking markers: every reference in a grouped citation like [8, 13] is audited against the exact sentence INDEPENDENTLY, so group them only where EACH abstract supports that whole sentence on its own. Where two papers support different halves of a point, write two sentences with one marker each. This is the single most common reason a draft is sent back.
RESULTS. Walk the reader through the evidence: discuss each figure and each table where it is relevant to the point being made, rather than listing them at the end.
DO NOT RESTATE THE CONFIGURATION. The dataset, split, architecture, training budget and outcome definition are written for you into the Experimental Setup and the appendix. State them nowhere else — not in the Method, not a second time in the setup.
WHAT THE SETUP SECTION IS FOR, then, is the DESIGN and its justification, and it still owes the reader 300-500 words of it: why a subject-disjoint split tests what this question asks and what a random split would have hidden; what pairing every condition on one seed buys and what it costs; what each negative control rules out and what would have been indistinguishable without it; why this many seeds; what the analysis does with them. None of that is in the configuration block, and a reader cannot infer it from the numbers.
The METHOD is about the OPERATOR — what it does, why that is the right expression of the hypothesis, and what its comparator neutralises.
The CONCLUSION (150-250 words) states what was found, what it changes for someone choosing between these methods, and what would settle the question next. Not a one-paragraph restatement of the abstract.
NAME THE ARMS AS THE TABLES DO: 'the proposed condition', 'the baseline', 'the first negative control', 'the second negative control'. Do not invent a parallel name such as 'Intervention' — the reader has to match your prose to the tables.
REGISTER. Never enumerate random seeds in the prose — they are in the appendix. Never annotate a sentence with the subsystem that produced it.

[claim-language] Claim what the evidence carries, and no more. Keep four registers apart and make it obvious which one a sentence is in: a RESULT states a measured quantity; an INTERPRETATION says what it may mean and is marked as such ('suggests', 'is consistent with'); a LIMITATION says what this design cannot tell anyone; FUTURE WORK proposes what would settle the question, and is the only register in which a wider setting may appear.
